+}

🔴 DB errors in the new brokercore package are silently collapsed into semantic 4xx sentinels across five code paths in credential.go and session.go, causing infrastructure failures to masquerade as client errors. Agents receiving a misleading 403 "No broker service configured" or 400 "set vault hint" will not back off or retry as they would for a 5xx, and operators see no signal of a system-level outage; each err \!= nil arm should return a wrapped internal error so WriteInjectError/writeAuthError fall through to their 500 default cases while the v == nil/cfg == nil/role == "" arms correctly retain the semantic sentinels.

<details>
<summary>Extended reasoning...</summary>

What the bug is and how it manifests

In internal/brokercore/credential.go (line 47-50) and internal/brokercore/session.go (three locations), every store call conflates two very different failure modes into a single sentinel error: (a) a legitimate "not configured / not found" result (e.g. sql.ErrNoRows), and (b) a genuine DB error (connectivity loss, locked database, I/O failure). Because the code collapses both into the same sentinel, callers and HTTP handlers cannot distinguish an infrastructure outage from a missing record, and both end up producing an HTTP 4xx response.

The specific code paths

credential.go line 47: if err \!= nil || cfg == nil { return nil, ErrServiceNotFound }. ErrServiceNotFound maps through WriteInjectError to HTTP 403 with a proposal_hint body. In session.go: (1) GetVaultByID: if err \!= nil || v == nil { return nil, ErrVaultNotFound } maps to 404 "vault not found"; (2) GetVault (hint path): same pattern, also 404; (3) GetVaultRole: if err \!= nil || role == "" { return nil, ErrVaultAccessDenied } maps to 403 "forbidden"; (4) ListActorGrants: if err \!= nil { return nil, ErrNoVaultContext } maps to 400 "set vault via HTTPS_PROXY=http://token:vault@host:port".

Why existing code does not prevent it

The SQLite implementation of scanBrokerConfig returns (nil, err) for both sql.ErrNoRows and real DB errors -- it never returns (nil, nil). This means the cfg == nil branch in Inject is dead code; only the err \!= nil branch fires. Both the legitimate "no service configured" case and a hard DB failure hit the same ErrServiceNotFound return. The same pattern holds for scanVault and GetVaultRole: a successful scan always populates the struct/string, so the nil/empty-string guards are effectively dead code for the success path, and the error path swallows the real failure.

What the impact would be

An agent hitting a transient DB outage (SQLite locked, connection closed, disk I/O error) on the credential-injection path would receive HTTP 403 with a proposal_hint body suggesting it create a new broker service -- one that may already exist. The agent, following the hint, might file redundant proposals. Operators monitoring HTTP status distributions see no 5xx spike, so the DB problem may go unnoticed. On the session-resolution paths: an agent might be told its vault does not exist (404) or that it is forbidden (403) when the real problem is a DB failure, suppressing any retry or alerting logic that keys on 5xx.

How to fix it

Split the error-check and nil-check arms for each store call. For credential.go: guard err \!= nil with fmt.Errorf("brokercore: GetBrokerConfig: %w", err) which returns an unwrapped internal error that falls through to the 500 default in WriteInjectError, while keeping cfg == nil as the ErrServiceNotFound sentinel. Apply the same pattern to each of the four session.go paths: guard err \!= nil with a wrapped internal error (falling through to writeAuthError default 500 case), and keep the v == nil / role == "" checks as the semantic sentinels.

Step-by-step proof

Suppose the SQLite file is locked (e.g. a backup is running). An agent sends CONNECT api.example.com:443 with a valid session to the MITM proxy. handleConnect calls sessions.ResolveForProxy which succeeds in getting the session (VaultID = "v1"). Code then calls r.Store.GetVaultByID(ctx, "v1"). SQLite returns (nil, error: database is locked). The check if err \!= nil || v == nil fires, returning ErrVaultNotFound. writeAuthError maps ErrVaultNotFound to http.Error(w, "vault not found", 404). The agent HTTP client does not retry (4xx = client error), logs "vault not found", and alerts its operator that the vault was deleted. The actual vault exists; only the DB was temporarily locked. The operator sees no 5xx in metrics, the DB issue goes uninvestigated, and the agent remains offline.

</details>

🟡 The 400 error message for global user login sessions (no vault scope) tells users to add a vault hint via `HTTPS_PROXY=http://<token>:<vault>@host:port`, but this hint only works for agent tokens — user sessions always hit the early `sess.AgentID == ""` guard in `ResolveForProxy` before reaching vault-hint logic, producing the same 400 again in an infinite confusion loop. The correct guidance is to create a scoped session via `POST /v1/sessions` before using the proxy.

<details>
<summary>Extended reasoning...</summary>

**What the bug is:** In `internal/mitm/connect.go`, `writeAuthError` maps both `ErrAgentVaultAmbiguous` and `ErrNoVaultContext` to the same HTTP 400 response: `set vault via HTTPS_PROXY=http://<token>:<vault>@host:port`. This message is only actionable for the `ErrAgentVaultAmbiguous` case (an instance-level agent token with multiple vault grants that hasn't specified which vault to use).

**The specific code path:** In `internal/brokercore/session.go` lines 112–114, when a session has `VaultID == ""` (not a scoped session), the resolver checks `sess.AgentID == ""` before examining any vault hint. A global user login session (UserID set, VaultID empty, AgentID empty) hits this guard and immediately returns `ErrNoVaultContext`.

**Why existing code doesn't prevent it:** The vault-hint resolution branch (`if vaultHint \!= ""` at line 96) lives *after* the `AgentID == ""` guard. Because user sessions have no AgentID, they never reach vault-hint logic regardless of what userinfo is in the HTTPS_PROXY URL. `ErrNoVaultContext` is reused for two distinct situations: (1) agent token with zero grants, and (2) user session with no vault scope — but only situation (1) can be resolved by adding a vault hint.

**Step-by-step proof of confusion loop:** User has global login token `av_user_tok` (UserID=u1, VaultID=empty, AgentID=empty). Step 1: `HTTPS_PROXY=http://av_user_tok@...` → `ParseProxyAuth` gets token=`av_user_tok`, vaultHint=`""`. `ResolveForProxy` sees `VaultID==""`, checks `sess.AgentID==""` → returns `ErrNoVaultContext`. `writeAuthError` emits HTTP 400: `set vault via HTTPS_PROXY=http://<token>:<vault>@host:port`. Step 2: User follows instruction, tries `HTTPS_PROXY=http://av_user_tok:default@...` → `ResolveForProxy` again sees `VaultID==""`, checks `sess.AgentID==""` → returns `ErrNoVaultContext` again, vault hint never examined. Same 400, same useless message. The test `TestResolveForProxy_UserSessionNoVaultNoAgent` confirms this code path is intentional — the rejection is correct, but the error message is not.

**Impact:** Any user attempting to use a global login token with the MITM proxy receives permanently-ineffective advice, with no way out via the error message.

**How to fix:** Introduce a separate sentinel error (e.g. `ErrUserSessionNoVaultScope`) for the user-session-without-vault path, and map it in `writeAuthError` to: `user sessions require vault scope; create a scoped session via POST /v1/sessions`. Alternatively, make the shared `ErrNoVaultContext` message more generic so it doesn't imply a vault hint will help.

</details>

body:
🟡 This PR adds a new public HTTP endpoint (GET /v1/mitm/ca.pem) and CLI command (agent-vault ca fetch) without updating cmd/skill_cli.md or cmd/skill_http.md, violating the CLAUDE.md convention that both skill files must be updated together whenever the agent-facing API surface changes. While the CA cert setup is primarily an operator step rather than an automated agent workflow, the omission leaves the skill files incomplete relative to the project's own documentation standard.

<details>
<summary>Extended reasoning...</summary>

CLAUDE.md states: "After notable changes, update both cmd/skill_cli.md and cmd/skill_http.md if the change affects the agent-facing API surface (e.g. new/changed endpoints, response fields, request constraints). Both skill files must be updated together." This PR introduces two new user-facing additions: the public HTTP endpoint GET /v1/mitm/ca.pem (registered in internal/server/server.go:614) and the CLI command "agent-vault ca fetch" (cmd/ca.go). Neither cmd/skill_cli.md nor cmd/skill_http.md was updated to document these.

The refuting verifiers argue that the CLAUDE.md qualifier "if the change affects the agent-facing API surface" excludes this endpoint because CA cert installation is an operator setup step, not part of an agent automated workflow (discover -> proxy -> propose). They point out that other operational endpoints like /health are absent from skill files, and that no AI agent would call GET /v1/mitm/ca.pem during task execution. This argument has real merit.

However, the confirming verifiers position is also sound: CLAUDE.md explicitly calls out "new/changed endpoints" as an example of what triggers the update requirement, and this is unambiguously a new public endpoint. The skill files serve as the authoritative reference for what agents need to know, and an agent launched into an environment where HTTPS_PROXY is set would need to know how to establish CA trust before any proxied HTTPS connections succeed.

The concrete impact: an agent relying on skill_cli.md to understand available commands has no way to discover "agent-vault ca fetch", and one relying on skill_http.md has no way to discover GET /v1/mitm/ca.pem — both directly relevant to making the MITM proxy feature usable.

Step-by-step proof: (1) CLAUDE.md defines the convention at the Conventions section. (2) cmd/ca.go adds "agent-vault ca fetch" and registers it in rootCmd via init(). (3) internal/server/server.go line 614 registers "GET /v1/mitm/ca.pem" in the HTTP mux. (4) A grep for "ca.pem", "ca fetch", or "mitm" in cmd/skill_cli.md and cmd/skill_http.md returns no results. (5) Therefore, the CLAUDE.md convention was not followed.

The fix: add a short section to cmd/skill_cli.md documenting "agent-vault ca fetch" and a corresponding entry in cmd/skill_http.md documenting "GET /v1/mitm/ca.pem", both gated on the server being started with --mitm-port. This is a documentation/process miss rather than a functional bug.

</details>

🔴 When the MITM proxy fails to bind (e.g. port 14322 already in use), two problems occur: (1) "Agent Vault transparent proxy listening on 127.0.0.1:14322" is printed before `ListenAndServe` is called, so a port conflict produces contradictory output — a success message immediately followed by a warning. (2) More critically, `s.mitm` remains non-nil after the bind failure (it was set in `attachMITMIfEnabled` before `Start()` is called), so `GET /v1/mitm/ca.pem` still returns a valid PEM with HTTP 200 even though nothing is listening on port 14322. An operator who runs `agent-vault ca fetch`, installs the certificate, and sets `HTTPS_PROXY` will receive silent connection-refused errors with no indication the proxy never started — a confusing failure mode that is directly introduced by making bind failures non-fatal in this PR.

<details>
<summary>Extended reasoning...</summary>

**Bug 1 — premature "listening on" message (nit)**

Line 706 prints "Agent Vault transparent proxy listening on 127.0.0.1:14322" *before* calling `s.mitm.ListenAndServe()` on line 707. If the port is already in use, the goroutine immediately prints the warning on stderr, producing output like:

```
Agent Vault transparent proxy listening on 127.0.0.1:14322
warning: transparent proxy unavailable: listen tcp 127.0.0.1:14322: bind: address already in use
```

The first line signals success; the second signals failure. An operator scanning startup logs sees a contradictory state. The same print-before-bind pattern exists for the main HTTP server goroutine (line 695/699), but there a bind failure propagates via `errCh` and terminates the process, so the contradiction is brief and obvious. For MITM the error is now swallowed, so the misleading "listening on" line persists in the log with no retraction.

**Bug 2 — `/v1/mitm/ca.pem` serves PEM when proxy is not listening (normal)**

The lifecycle sequence is:
1. `attachMITMIfEnabled` (called before `Start()`) creates the proxy and calls `s.AttachMITM(p)`, setting `s.mitm = p`.
2. Inside `Start()`, the goroutine calls `s.mitm.ListenAndServe()`. If this fails (port conflict), the goroutine logs to stderr and exits — but `s.mitm` is **never cleared**.
3. `handleMITMCA` in `handle_mitm.go` gates the 404 response with `if s.mitm == nil`. Since `s.mitm` is non-nil (set in step 1), the condition is never true, and `s.mitm.RootPEM()` is returned unconditionally.
4. `Proxy.RootPEM()` calls `p.ca.RootPEM()` with no listening-state check — it returns valid PEM bytes regardless of whether `ListenAndServe` ever succeeded.

**Why existing code doesn't prevent this**

Before this PR, a MITM bind failure sent the error to `errCh`, which caused `Start()` to return an error and terminate the server. This made the "s.mitm non-nil but not listening" state unreachable. The PR's non-fatal redesign (changing `errCh <- fmt.Errorf(...)" to a stderr warning) introduced the reachable gap without updating the CA endpoint's gating logic.

**Concrete proof**

1. Start a first instance: `agent-vault server` — binds core HTTP on 14321 and MITM on 14322.
2. Start a second instance: `agent-vault server` — core HTTP bind on 14321 fails and terminates the process; but if 14321 were available (e.g. different port) and only 14322 were taken, the second instance would start with `s.mitm` non-nil but nothing listening on 14322.
3. `agent-vault ca fetch` against the second instance returns HTTP 200 with a valid PEM.
4. Operator installs the PEM into their trust store and sets `HTTPS_PROXY=http://localhost:14322`.
5. Every HTTPS request gets "connection refused" on port 14322, with no useful diagnostic — the warning was only printed at server startup on stderr, not surfaced to the CA fetch caller.

**Fix**

Track whether `ListenAndServe` successfully bound: use an atomic boolean or a channel that the goroutine signals on first successful accept (or after a brief listen-without-error period). Alternatively, set `s.mitm = nil` in the goroutine *before* logging the warning (requires a mutex since `handleMITMCA` reads `s.mitm` concurrently). The simplest safe fix is to add an `isListening atomic.Bool` to `mitm.Proxy`, set it to true inside `ListenAndServe` after the listener is created but before the accept loop, and check it in `handleMITMCA` alongside the nil check.

</details>

🔴 CA initialization failures in `attachMITMIfEnabled` are still fatal server startup errors, even though this PR made port-bind failures non-fatal. Since the default `--mitm-port` is now 14322 (not 0), `ca.New()` runs on every fresh server start — any filesystem permission error on `~/.agent-vault/ca/`, corrupted CA files, or key derivation failure will prevent the core HTTP server from starting at all. The error message (`init CA: <reason>`) gives no hint that `--mitm-port 0` is a workaround.

<details>
<summary>Extended reasoning...</summary>

**What the bug is and how it manifests**

The PR changes the default value of `--mitm-port` from `0` to `DefaultMITMPort` (14322) in `cmd/server.go init()`. This means `attachMITMIfEnabled` is now called on every server start rather than only when the user explicitly opts in. Inside `attachMITMIfEnabled` (cmd/server.go ~line 133-145), `ca.New()` is called to load or create the root CA. If that call fails, the function returns `fmt.Errorf("init CA: %w", err)` — a hard error that propagates up through `serverCmd.RunE` and aborts the entire server process before the core HTTP server even binds.

**The specific code path that triggers it**

```
serverCmd.RunE
  → attachMITMIfEnabled(srv, host, mitmPort, masterKey.Key())
      → ca.New(masterKey, ca.Options{})   // can fail
      → return fmt.Errorf("init CA: %w", err)  // propagated as hard error
  → if err != nil { return err }          // server exits
```

The same is true in the detached-child path (`runDetachedChild`), which also calls `attachMITMIfEnabled` and propagates its error.

**Why existing code doesn't prevent it**

The PR correctly made `ListenAndServe` failures non-fatal — that error is now just logged to stderr as a warning (internal/server/server.go). But that only covers runtime bind conflicts. CA initialization happens earlier, before the proxy goroutine is ever started, and its error is still returned directly to the startup call site.

**Concrete failure scenarios for ca.New()**

1. `os.UserHomeDir()` fails — containers without `HOME` set (e.g., Docker images running as non-root with no homedir configured).
2. `os.MkdirAll("~/.agent-vault/ca/", ...)` fails — read-only filesystems, restrictive container security policies, or permission mismatches.
3. Corrupted or partially-written CA cert/key files — e.g., interrupted first-run initialization.
4. Wrong master key — re-setup after a `owner reset` leaves old encrypted CA files that can no longer be decrypted.

**Step-by-step proof**

Assume a container with no home directory (`HOME` unset):

1. User runs `agent-vault server` with no flags (new default: `--mitm-port 14322`).
2. `serverCmd.RunE` reaches `attachMITMIfEnabled(srv, host, 14322, key)`.
3. `ca.New()` calls `os.UserHomeDir()`, which returns an error (`$HOME not set`).
4. `attachMITMIfEnabled` returns `fmt.Errorf("init CA: $HOME not set")`.
5. `serverCmd.RunE` returns that error — cobra prints it and exits with code 1.
6. The core HTTP server never starts. Agent, vault, and proxy functionality is completely unavailable.
7. The user sees `Error: init CA: $HOME not set` with no hint that `--mitm-port 0` would let the server start normally.

**Before this PR**, the same container would have started successfully because the default was 0, `attachMITMIfEnabled` returned immediately, and `ca.New()` was never called.

**Impact**

This is a regression for any deployment environment that cannot create `~/.agent-vault/ca/` — containerized workloads, CI runners, restricted Linux accounts, and any environment that ran `agent-vault server` without issues before upgrading.

**How to fix**

Treat CA init failures with the same best-effort philosophy as bind failures: log a warning and skip the MITM proxy rather than aborting startup. For example:

```go
func attachMITMIfEnabled(srv *server.Server, host string, mitmPort int, masterKey []byte) error {
    if mitmPort <= 0 {
        return nil
    }
    caProv, err := ca.New(masterKey, ca.Options{})
    if err != nil {
        fmt.Fprintf(os.Stderr, "warning: transparent proxy disabled (CA init failed: %v); pass --mitm-port 0 to suppress\n", err)
        return nil  // non-fatal
    }
    srv.AttachMITM(mitm.New(...))
    return nil
}
```

</details>

body:
🟡 README.md was not updated to reflect the transparent MITM proxy being enabled by default on port 14322, violating CLAUDE.md's convention: "When a change affects operator-facing behavior, update README.md." The Docker example in README.md only exposes port 14321, so Docker users following the README will silently have an inaccessible MITM proxy. Operators reading only README.md will not know the proxy now runs by default, how to disable it (--mitm-port 0), or that they need to install a root CA cert.

<details>
<summary>Extended reasoning...</summary>

**What the bug is and how it manifests**

CLAUDE.md line 48 establishes a clear project convention: "When a change affects operator-facing behavior, update README.md." This PR flips the transparent MITM proxy from opt-in to the default behavior — every `agent-vault server` invocation now binds port 14322 and initializes an on-disk CA on first launch. That is a significant operator-facing behavioral change. README.md contains zero mentions of 'mitm', 'transparent', or '14322' (verified by the verifiers with grep across 134 lines). The convention was violated.

**The specific code path and concrete proof**

Consider an operator who reads only README.md and follows its Docker quick-start, which shows `-p 14321:14321`. They start the server:

1. `agent-vault server` now silently binds port 14322 for the MITM proxy in addition to 14321.
2. Because the Docker run command only maps `-p 14321:14321`, port 14322 is not exposed to the host.
3. The MITM proxy starts inside the container but is unreachable from outside.
4. `agent-vault ca fetch` from the host will succeed (it hits 14321/v1/mitm/ca.pem), but setting HTTPS_PROXY to the container on port 14322 silently fails — no traffic proxied.
5. The operator has no README.md hint that they need to add `-p 14322:14322` or run `--mitm-port 0` to disable.

For non-Docker operators: they will see a second port appear on their server and wonder what it is, or receive a CA initialization error with no README.md explanation.

**Why existing code doesn't prevent it**

The non-fatal MITM bind failure (added in this PR) only prevents the *entire process* from dying — it does not surface any operator-visible documentation gap. The --help flag and docs/reference/cli.mdx do reflect the new default, but README.md is the first touchpoint for most operators and remains out of date.

**Addressing the refutation**

The refutation argues that since README.md never covered MITM when it was opt-in, there is nothing to "update." This reasoning does not hold: when a feature transitions from opt-in to *default-on*, it changes from something operators can ignore to something that affects every operator on every server start. The CLAUDE.md convention was written precisely to catch this: behavioral changes require README.md updates. The fact that the docs/self-hosting/local.mdx and docs/reference/cli.mdx were updated demonstrates the team knew this was operator-facing; README.md was simply overlooked.

**Impact**

Docker operators following README.md verbatim will have a silently broken MITM proxy. Bare-metal operators will see an unexplained second port and CA initialization without guidance. The `--mitm-port 0` opt-out is undiscoverable from README.md alone.

**How to fix**

Add a brief note to README.md's server startup section mentioning that a transparent MITM proxy listens on port 14322 by default, that it can be disabled with `--mitm-port 0`, and that clients need the root CA installed. Update the Docker example to expose `-p 14322:14322` or note that `--mitm-port 0` can suppress it in Docker deployments.

</details>

🟣 The `--host` flag default is documented as `localhost` in the CLI reference table, but the actual default defined in `cmd/defaults.go` is `127.0.0.1`. This is a pre-existing discrepancy that was not fixed when this PR modified the neighboring `--mitm-port` row in the same table. With the transparent MITM proxy now enabled by default on this host, operators configuring firewall rules or `HTTPS_PROXY` URLs based on the documented `localhost` value may encounter unexpected behavior on dual-stack systems where `localhost` resolves to `::1` (IPv6) rather than `127.0.0.1` (IPv4).

<details>
<summary>Extended reasoning...</summary>

**What the bug is:** `docs/reference/cli.mdx` documents the `--host` flag default as `localhost` (line 20), but the actual default is `127.0.0.1` as defined by `DefaultHost` in `cmd/defaults.go` line 5, and registered as the flag default in `cmd/server.go` line 504 (`serverCmd.Flags().String("host", DefaultHost, "host to bind to")`).

**Why localhost ≠ 127.0.0.1:** On modern Linux and macOS systems, `/etc/hosts` (or `nsswitch.conf`) commonly maps `localhost` to both `127.0.0.1` and `::1`. When Go's net resolver picks `localhost`, it may return the IPv6 address `::1` first. A server bound to `127.0.0.1` is an IPv4 loopback socket that does NOT accept connections on `::1`. These are distinct bind addresses for firewall rules, dual-stack routing, and `HTTPS_PROXY` URL construction.

**Why this PR increases the relevance:** The transparent MITM proxy is now enabled by default and also binds to `DefaultHost` (127.0.0.1). Any operator who reads the docs, sees `localhost` as the default, and constructs firewall rules or `HTTPS_PROXY=http://...` URLs with `localhost` will be working from incorrect information. Previously (MITM opt-in) the blast radius was smaller; with MITM now default-on, more operators encounter this binding for the first time via the docs.

**Step-by-step proof:**
1. Operator reads `docs/reference/cli.mdx` and sees `--host` default = `localhost`.
2. Operator writes an iptables/nftables rule allowing connections to `::1:14322` (the IPv6 loopback address of `localhost` on their system).
3. Actual server binds to `127.0.0.1:14322` (IPv4) — the firewall rule never matches.
4. Alternatively, operator sets `HTTPS_PROXY=http://localhost:14322` — the client resolves `localhost` to `::1`, tries to connect to `[::1]:14322`, and gets a connection refused error because the server only listens on `127.0.0.1`.

**Why existing code doesn't prevent it:** The docs are manually maintained and the discrepancy was present before this PR. The PR author edited the same table (the `--mitm-port` row immediately below) without noticing or correcting the adjacent `--host` row.

**Fix:** Change the `--host` row in the `docs/reference/cli.mdx` table from `localhost` to `127.0.0.1` to match `DefaultHost` in `cmd/defaults.go`.

</details>

🔴 In handleProxy, event.Path is initialized to r.URL.Path (e.g. /proxy/api.github.com/v1/users) and never corrected after the host/path are parsed out, so the explicit ingress logs path=/proxy/api.github.com/v1/users while the MITM ingress logs path=/v1/users. The fix is to add event.Path = "/" + remainingPath (handling the empty-path case) after the line that sets event.Host = targetHost.

<details>
<summary>Extended reasoning...</summary>

The bug is in internal/server/handle_proxy.go. At handler entry, ProxyEvent is initialized with Path: r.URL.Path, which for an explicit proxy request is the full handler path /proxy/api.github.com/v1/users. This is a routing artifact — the Go mux matched the /proxy/ prefix and r.URL.Path still carries it verbatim.

Later in the same function, the code parses out the upstream coordinates with strings.Cut(trimmed, "/"), producing targetHost = "api.github.com" and remainingPath = "v1/users". The field event.Host is correctly updated to targetHost, but event.Path is never updated. It remains /proxy/api.github.com/v1/users for the lifetime of the request.

In the MITM path (internal/mitm/forward.go), the ProxyEvent is initialized with Path: r.URL.Path inside the inner HTTP/1.1 handler that runs after the CONNECT tunnel is established. At that point the HTTP request inside the tunnel is already a normal upstream request, so r.URL.Path is /v1/users — the upstream path only. The two code paths are structurally parallel, but the explicit ingress logs a structurally different path field.

The PR description explicitly promises: "both ingress paths (explicit /proxy/ and transparent MITM) emit one structured slog line per request: ingress, method, host, path, matched broker service...". The inconsistency directly contradicts this claim: consumers parsing the debug logs (dashboards, log aggregators, jq filters) cannot treat path uniformly across both ingress types.

Step-by-step proof:
1. Agent sends GET /proxy/api.github.com/v1/users with a bearer session token.
2. handleProxy is entered; r.URL.Path = "/proxy/api.github.com/v1/users".
3. ProxyEvent{Path: r.URL.Path} is set, so Path = "/proxy/api.github.com/v1/users".
4. trimmed = "api.github.com/v1/users", targetHost = "api.github.com", remainingPath = "v1/users".
5. event.Host = targetHost sets host correctly.
6. event.Path is never updated.
7. Handler proceeds through auth, credential injection, upstream round-trip, and calls emit(resp.StatusCode, "").
8. LogProxyEvent is called with path="/proxy/api.github.com/v1/users".
9. For the same upstream resource via MITM: Path is set from the inner-tunnel r.URL.Path = "/v1/users", so the log emits path=/v1/users.

Fix: Add event.Path = "/" + remainingPath (or event.Path = "/" when remainingPath is empty) immediately after event.Host = targetHost. This mirrors how the outbound targetURL is constructed a few lines later.

</details>

🟡 The `make dev` target sets `AGENT_VAULT_LOG_LEVEL` from the shell env before sourcing `.env`, so a value in `.env` silently overwrites an explicit shell env value — the opposite of the documented behavior. The fix is to source `.env` first, then apply the `:-debug` default so the shell env wins over both `.env` and the default.

<details>
<summary>Extended reasoning...</summary>

What the bug is: In the Makefile `dev` target, the comment states "an explicit value in the shell env or .env file wins", implying shell env has at least equal priority to `.env`. However, the actual execution order is: (1) `export AGENT_VAULT_LOG_LEVEL=${AGENT_VAULT_LOG_LEVEL:-debug}` captures the current shell value or defaults to `debug`; (2) `set -a; . ./.env; set +a` sources `.env` and re-exports every variable defined in it, unconditionally overwriting anything set in step 1.

The specific code path that triggers it: A developer runs `AGENT_VAULT_LOG_LEVEL=info make dev` to suppress debug logs. The shell env sets the variable to `info` in step 1. But their team shared `.env` file contains `AGENT_VAULT_LOG_LEVEL=debug`. In step 2, `set -a; . ./.env; set +a` sources the file and exports `AGENT_VAULT_LOG_LEVEL=debug`, overwriting the developer explicit `info` setting. The final value passed to `air` is `debug`.

Why existing code does not prevent it: The `:-debug` Bash expansion is evaluated once at step 1 time. After that, `AGENT_VAULT_LOG_LEVEL` holds the resolved value (`info`). When `.env` is sourced with `set -a`, the shell reassigns the variable if the file defines it — there is no guard against overwriting. The comment acknowledges the intent but the implementation does not enforce it.

Impact: A developer who sets `AGENT_VAULT_LOG_LEVEL=info` in their shell to quiet the per-request debug logs will see them anyway because their team `.env` overrides their explicit preference. Conversely, a developer running `infisical run -- make dev` (which injects env vars) could have those values silently overridden by `.env`. This only affects the `make dev` convenience target and has no impact on production deployments.

How to fix it: Swap the two lines — source `.env` first, then apply the `:-debug` default. Now the priority is: shell env > .env > default(debug), which matches the documented intent and the standard dotenv convention.

Step-by-step proof: Suppose shell has `AGENT_VAULT_LOG_LEVEL=info` and `.env` contains `AGENT_VAULT_LOG_LEVEL=debug`. Current code: step 1 captures `info` from shell. Step 2 sources `.env` with `set -a`, which sets `AGENT_VAULT_LOG_LEVEL=debug` and exports it, overwriting `info`. Final value: `debug`. Expected: `info`. With the fix: step 1 sources `.env` (sets `AGENT_VAULT_LOG_LEVEL=debug` in subshell), but the shell env `info` value was already present before sourcing, so the shell variable retains `info`. Step 2 evaluates `${AGENT_VAULT_LOG_LEVEL:-debug}` — variable is already `info`, so no change. Final value: `info`. Correct.

</details>

🔴 augmentEnvWithMITM appends HTTPS_PROXY, HTTP_PROXY, SSL_CERT_FILE, and related variables to env (which starts as os.Environ()) without first removing any pre-existing instances of those keys. In environments where the parent shell already has HTTPS_PROXY or SSL_CERT_FILE set (e.g., corporate networks with a proxy or CA bundle), the child process inherits both the old and new values as duplicate entries. Because POSIX-compliant getenv() / glibc returns the *first* match, C and curl-based tools silently use the parent's proxy setting and ignore the injected MITM proxy URL, bypassing credential injection entirely. The fix is to strip existing occurrences of each injected key from env before appending the new values.

<details>
<summary>Extended reasoning...</summary>

**What the bug is and how it manifests**

`augmentEnvWithMITM` (cmd/run.go:277-333) receives `env`, which was populated with `os.Environ()` at line 87 of `runCmd`. It then blindly appends eight key=value pairs — `HTTPS_PROXY`, `HTTP_PROXY`, `NO_PROXY`, `SSL_CERT_FILE`, `NODE_EXTRA_CA_CERTS`, `REQUESTS_CA_BUNDLE`, `CURL_CA_BUNDLE`, `GIT_SSL_CAINFO` — using a single `append` call at lines 319-328. If any of these keys already appear in the parent process's environment (via `os.Environ()`), the resulting slice contains duplicate entries for those keys.

**The specific code path that triggers it**

`env := os.Environ()` at line 87 copies every variable from the parent shell verbatim. Three Agent Vault vars (`AGENT_VAULT_SESSION_TOKEN`, `AGENT_VAULT_ADDR`, `AGENT_VAULT_VAULT`) are appended first — those are new keys unlikely to conflict. But `augmentEnvWithMITM` then appends standard well-known proxy/CA vars without any de-duplication step. The `env` slice passed to `syscall.Exec` at line 120 therefore contains e.g. both `HTTPS_PROXY=http://corp-proxy:3128` (position N from the parent) and `HTTPS_PROXY=http://token:vault@127.0.0.1:14322` (position N+K, appended last).

**Why existing code does not prevent it**

There is no filtering or de-duplication anywhere between `os.Environ()` and the final `append`. The test helper `envMap` in `cmd/run_test.go` (line 141) stores values in a Go map with last-write-wins semantics, so the test suite always sees the new value — masking the issue for Go-native lookup semantics while the real problem only manifests in child processes that use C-library getenv.

**Impact**

POSIX specifies that the behavior of duplicate environment entries is undefined; in practice glibc's `getenv()` scans the `environ` array linearly and returns the **first** match. Go's `os.Getenv()` iterates from the end and returns the **last** match. This means: (1) For curl, bash, Python (libcurl backend), git, and any C-based tool — the parent's `HTTPS_PROXY` wins and all HTTPS traffic bypasses the MITM proxy, so credential injection never fires; (2) For the `SSL_CERT_FILE` case — if a corporate CA bundle was already set, C tools continue using that bundle and will fail TLS verification when connecting through the agent-vault MITM proxy (whose CA is not in the corporate bundle); (3) The tool appears to work correctly when tested with Go binaries, making the failure hard to reproduce and diagnose.

**Step-by-step proof**

Suppose the user's shell has `HTTPS_PROXY=http://corp:3128` and `SSL_CERT_FILE=/etc/ssl/corp-ca.pem`:
1. `env := os.Environ()` → env contains `[... "HTTPS_PROXY=http://corp:3128" ... "SSL_CERT_FILE=/etc/ssl/corp-ca.pem" ...]`
2. Agent Vault vars are appended → env grows by 3 entries, no conflict yet.
3. `augmentEnvWithMITM` writes `~/.agent-vault/mitm-ca.pem`, builds proxyURL, then calls `append(env, "HTTPS_PROXY="+proxyURL, ..., "SSL_CERT_FILE="+caPath, ...)`.
4. Resulting env slice: `[... "HTTPS_PROXY=http://corp:3128" ... "SSL_CERT_FILE=/etc/ssl/corp-ca.pem" ... "HTTPS_PROXY=http://token:vault@127.0.0.1:14322" ... "SSL_CERT_FILE=/root/.agent-vault/mitm-ca.pem" ...]`
5. `syscall.Exec(binary, args, env)` passes this slice directly to the kernel; the kernel stores it as-is.
6. Inside `curl` (glibc): `getenv("HTTPS_PROXY")` scans from index 0, finds `http://corp:3128` first, returns it. The MITM proxy is never used. No error is surfaced — HTTPS calls succeed but without credential injection.
7. `getenv("SSL_CERT_FILE")` similarly returns `/etc/ssl/corp-ca.pem`; the agent-vault CA is not trusted; any service the tool connects to via the MITM proxy will fail TLS verification.

**How to fix it**

Before the final `append` in `augmentEnvWithMITM`, filter `env` to remove any existing entries whose key matches one of the eight injected keys. A clean helper like:
```go
func filterEnvKeys(env []string, keys map[string]struct{}) []string {
    out := env[:0:len(env)]
    for _, kv := range env {
        if i := strings.IndexByte(kv, '='); i >= 0 {
            if _, drop := keys[kv[:i]]; drop { continue }
        }
        out = append(out, kv)
    }
    return out
}
```
ensures the new values are the only occurrences and behavior is consistent across all runtimes.

</details>

🔴 The proxy URL in augmentEnvWithMITM always uses DefaultMITMPort (14322) regardless of what port the server actually started on, so running 'agent-vault server --mitm-port 9000' causes the child process to receive HTTPS_PROXY pointing at port 14322 where nothing is listening. Since /v1/mitm/ca.pem only returns PEM bytes with no port information, the client has no way to discover the actual listening port; a server-side protocol change is needed (e.g., a response header or /v1/mitm/config endpoint).

<details>
<summary>Extended reasoning...</summary>

**What the bug is and how it manifests**

In augmentEnvWithMITM (cmd/run.go:315), the HTTPS_PROXY URL is built with a hardcoded constant:

```go
Host: fmt.Sprintf("%s:%d", mitmHost, DefaultMITMPort),
```

DefaultMITMPort is 14322 (cmd/defaults.go). This value is used unconditionally — there is no code path that reads the actual port the MITM proxy is listening on.

**The specific code path that triggers it**

A user runs: `agent-vault server --mitm-port 9000`. The server binds its transparent proxy on port 9000. Later, `agent-vault vault run -- bash` calls augmentEnvWithMITM, which calls fetchMITMCA. The /v1/mitm/ca.pem endpoint (internal/server/handle_mitm.go) returns 200 OK with the PEM body regardless of which port the proxy is on — the CA is a static certificate, independent of the listening port. fetchMITMCA returns (pem, true, nil). augmentEnvWithMITM proceeds to construct the proxy URL as `http://token:vault@127.0.0.1:14322` instead of `http://token:vault@127.0.0.1:9000`. This URL is injected into HTTPS_PROXY and HTTP_PROXY in the child's environment.

**Why existing code doesn't prevent it**

The /v1/mitm/ca.pem endpoint is the only server-side signal used to determine whether MITM is enabled. It returns only application/x-pem-file content — no X-MITM-Port header, no JSON wrapper, no link to another endpoint that would reveal the listening port. There is no /v1/mitm/config endpoint. The client therefore has zero mechanism to discover the actual port through this API.

**What the impact would be**

The child process sets HTTPS_PROXY to a URL pointing at a port where nothing is listening. Every HTTPS request from the child (curl, Python requests, Node.js https, git) will attempt to CONNECT through this proxy and receive a connection refused error. The failure mode depends on the HTTP client: some will surface a clear "connection refused" error; others may fall back to direct connections, silently bypassing the intended credential-injection proxy. In both cases, the core promise of the feature — transparent MITM credential injection — is broken for any deployment using a non-default MITM port.

**How to fix it**

The server needs to expose the actual listening port to the client. Two clean options: (1) Add an X-MITM-Port response header to /v1/mitm/ca.pem so the client can read it alongside the PEM; (2) Add a /v1/mitm/config endpoint that returns JSON including the port. The client side (augmentEnvWithMITM) then uses the returned port rather than DefaultMITMPort. A simpler but more fragile workaround would be a client-side --mitm-port flag for vault run, but that requires users to remember to pass the right port.

**Step-by-step proof**

1. Start server: `agent-vault server --mitm-port 9000` — proxy binds to :9000, not :14322.
2. Run: `agent-vault vault run -- env | grep PROXY`
3. augmentEnvWithMITM calls fetchMITMCA(addr) → GET /v1/mitm/ca.pem → 200 OK (CA is served regardless of port).
4. Code executes: `Host: fmt.Sprintf("%s:%d", mitmHost, DefaultMITMPort)` where DefaultMITMPort = 14322.
5. Child env receives: `HTTPS_PROXY=http://av_sess_xxx:default@127.0.0.1:14322`
6. Nothing is listening on :14322; all proxied HTTPS connections fail with connection refused.
7. The MITM proxy on :9000 never sees any traffic — credential injection is silently broken.

</details>

🔴 Setting `HTTP_PROXY` to the MITM proxy URL breaks all plain HTTP requests from child processes, because the MITM proxy only handles `CONNECT` tunnels and returns `405 Method Not Allowed` for every other method. Since the proxy is HTTPS-only by design, `HTTP_PROXY` should not be set — only `HTTPS_PROXY` should be exported.

<details>
<summary>Extended reasoning...</summary>

**What the bug is**

In `augmentEnvWithMITM` (cmd/run.go lines 318–321), both `HTTP_PROXY` and `HTTPS_PROXY` are set to the same proxy URL pointing at the MITM proxy. The MITM proxy is an HTTPS-only transparent interceptor — it is designed solely to intercept TLS traffic via HTTP CONNECT tunnels so it can inject credentials.

**The specific code path that triggers it**

```go
env = append(env,
    "HTTPS_PROXY="+proxyURL,
    "HTTP_PROXY="+proxyURL,   // <-- the bug
    ...
)
```

When `HTTP_PROXY` is set in the environment, standard HTTP clients (Go's `net/http`, Python `requests`, `curl`, etc.) route plain `http://` requests through the proxy using the absolute-URI form: e.g., `GET http://example.com/path HTTP/1.1`. This is a non-CONNECT request.

**Why existing code doesn't prevent it**

The MITM proxy's `dispatch` function (internal/mitm/proxy.go lines 115–121) has a hard check: it only handles `http.MethodConnect` and returns `405 Method Not Allowed` for everything else:

```go
http.Error(w, fmt.Sprintf("method %s not supported on transparent proxy", r.Method), http.StatusMethodNotAllowed)
```

There is no fallback, no passthrough, and no plain-HTTP proxying. The 405 is terminal.

**What the impact would be**

Any child process spawned by `vault run` that makes a plain `http://` request — including `curl http://...`, Python `requests.get('http://...')`, package managers hitting HTTP mirrors, Go `http.Get`, or any tool that uses `HTTP_PROXY` — will have its request rejected with 405. This is a silent, hard failure that will appear as a mysterious connection error to the child, not as an obvious proxy configuration problem.

**How to fix it**

Remove the `HTTP_PROXY=` line from the `env = append(env, ...)` call in `augmentEnvWithMITM`. The MITM proxy is HTTPS-only; plain HTTP requests should flow directly (or be excluded via `NO_PROXY`). Only `HTTPS_PROXY` should be set to the MITM proxy URL.

**Step-by-step proof**

1. User runs: `agent-vault vault run -- bash`
2. `augmentEnvWithMITM` succeeds; child bash inherits `HTTP_PROXY=http://av_sess_abc:default@127.0.0.1:14322`
3. Inside bash, user runs: `curl http://api.example.com/health`
4. `curl` sees `HTTP_PROXY`, routes the request to `127.0.0.1:14322` as: `GET http://api.example.com/health HTTP/1.1`
5. The MITM proxy receives the request; `dispatch` checks `r.Method == http.MethodConnect` — false
6. Proxy responds: `HTTP/1.1 405 Method Not Allowed` with body `method GET not supported on transparent proxy`
7. `curl` exits with an error. Any plain HTTP API call, package manager update, or webhook from the child is broken.

</details>

🔴 The new passthrough description in both skill_http.md (line 133) and skill_cli.md (line 114) claims "the client's `Authorization` and other request headers flow through unchanged," but this is only true for the MITM ingress (port 14322). On the explicit `/proxy/{host}/{path}` ingress, `handle_proxy.go` passes `"Authorization"` as an `extraStrip` argument to `ApplyInjection`, so `Authorization` is always removed even for passthrough services — because on that ingress it carries the AV session token. Agents relying on this documentation to forward an upstream Authorization header via `/proxy` will have it silently stripped, causing unexpected 401s from upstream with no clear error message. The correct guidance (use the MITM ingress for passthrough services that need to forward Authorization) exists only in a code comment at `handle_proxy.go:190-194` and never surfaces in the agent-facing skill docs.

<details>
<summary>Extended reasoning...</summary>

**What the bug is and how it manifests**

Both `skill_http.md` and `skill_cli.md` describe passthrough auth as forwarding the client's `Authorization` header to the upstream unchanged. The new passthrough paragraph in `skill_http.md` (line 133) states: *"the client's `Authorization` and other request headers flow through unchanged (hop-by-hop headers, `X-Vault`, and `Proxy-Authorization` are still stripped)."* `skill_cli.md` (line 114) makes the same claim without even the parenthetical qualifier. Both statements are factually wrong for the explicit `/proxy/{host}/{path}` ingress that both skill docs primarily describe.

**The specific code path that triggers it**

In `internal/server/handle_proxy.go`, the outbound headers are built by calling:
```go
brokercore.ApplyInjection(r.Header, outReq.Header, inject, "Authorization")
```
The fourth argument, `"Authorization"`, is the `extraStrip` list fed to `CopyPassthroughRequestHeaders`. When `inject.Passthrough` is `true`, `ApplyInjection` calls `CopyPassthroughRequestHeaders(src, dst, "Authorization")`, which explicitly drops `Authorization` before copying any other headers. This applies unconditionally — there is no fast-path that preserves `Authorization` for passthrough services on this ingress. By contrast, the MITM ingress in `internal/mitm/forward.go` calls `brokercore.ApplyInjection(r.Header, outReq.Header, inject)` with **no** `extraStrip` argument, so `Authorization` flows through unchanged there.

**Why existing code doesn't prevent it**

The code comment at `handle_proxy.go:190-194` is correct and explicit: *"Authorization carries the Agent Vault session token on this ingress; strip it on passthrough so the session credential never reaches the target. Clients needing to forward an upstream Authorization should use the MITM ingress."* The test `TestProxyPassthroughForwardsClientHeaders` in `server_test.go` likewise asserts that `Authorization` IS stripped on the `/proxy` ingress for passthrough services. The implementation and tests are consistent and correct. The problem is purely in the agent-facing documentation, which makes the opposite claim.

**What the impact would be**

An agent reading `skill_http.md` (the HTTP-API skill used by agents without the CLI binary) configures a passthrough service and sends `Authorization: Bearer upstream-token` on a `/proxy/{host}` request, expecting it to reach the upstream. Instead, `Authorization` is silently stripped. The upstream returns `401 Unauthorized`. Agent Vault returns the upstream 401 to the agent with no `X-Agent-Vault-Proxy-Error` header and no agent-readable indication that the header was dropped — the agent has no way to distinguish "upstream rejected my token" from "my token was never sent." Agents reading `skill_cli.md` that use the explicit `/proxy` endpoint (also documented in that file) face the same problem.

**How to fix it**

Both passthrough paragraphs should be qualified with the ingress distinction that the code and PR description already document clearly. For `skill_http.md` (which describes the `/proxy` HTTP API), the paragraph should note that Authorization is stripped on `/proxy` and that agents needing to forward an upstream Authorization header must use the MITM ingress (`HTTPS_PROXY`) instead. For `skill_cli.md`, the same qualification applies. The PR description's own Semantics section already documents this distinction correctly per-ingress; the skill docs need to surface it.

**Step-by-step proof**

1. Operator creates a passthrough service: `vault service add --host api.example.com --auth-type passthrough`
2. Agent reads `skill_http.md` and concludes: *"Authorization flows through unchanged"*.
3. Agent sends: `GET /proxy/api.example.com/data` with headers `Authorization: Bearer av_sess_xxx` (session auth) and — trying to forward an upstream credential — the agent might instead rely on `skill_http.md`'s claim and set an upstream-specific Authorization after AV processes the session token. In practice the agent sends one `Authorization` header (its session token) which AV uses for auth, then expects to also forward an upstream token; or uses a pattern where the same header carries both intents.
4. `handleProxy` authenticates the session from `Authorization: Bearer av_sess_xxx`, then calls `ApplyInjection(..., inject, "Authorization")`.
5. `CopyPassthroughRequestHeaders` strips `Authorization` because it is in `extraStrip`.
6. The upstream receives the request with **no** `Authorization` header and returns `401`.
7. The agent receives a bare `401` with no proxy-layer explanation. The agent is misled because `skill_http.md` told it Authorization would flow through. Silent auth failure.

</details>

🟡 The sawProxyAuth assertion in TestMITMPassthroughForwardsClientAuthorization is vacuous — Go's http.Transport sends Proxy-Authorization only on the CONNECT handshake (via url.User), not on subsequent in-tunnel requests, so sawProxyAuth is always empty regardless of whether CopyPassthroughRequestHeaders strips it. To make the assertion meaningful, the test should explicitly set req.Header.Set("Proxy-Authorization", "Basic xxx") on the inner request before sending.

<details>
<summary>Extended reasoning...</summary>

What the bug is. TestMITMPassthroughForwardsClientAuthorization creates an HTTP client via newTrustingClient(proxyURL, url.User("av_sess_ok"), clientRoots). The url.User field causes Go's http.Transport to emit Proxy-Authorization: Basic <base64> on the CONNECT request to establish the tunnel. Once the tunnel is up, in-tunnel requests are ordinary HTTP/1.1 requests — the transport does NOT re-send Proxy-Authorization on them. The test never calls req.Header.Set("Proxy-Authorization", ...) on the inner request object, so the upstream handler always sees an empty value in sawProxyAuth.

The specific code path. Lines ~256-272 of internal/mitm/proxy_test.go: the upstream handler records r.Header.Get("Proxy-Authorization") into sawProxyAuth, but the inner request r is the tunneled request sent inside the HTTPS connection — it is constructed from the req object that has only Authorization, Cookie, and X-Trace-Id headers set. Proxy-Authorization is absent by construction, not because the proxy stripped it.

Why existing code does not prevent this. The test comment says "Proxy-Authorization and hop-by-hop headers must still be stripped," which creates the impression of a meaningful guard. But the guard if sawProxyAuth != "" { t.Fatalf(...) } can never trigger because the header is never populated in the tunneled request in the first place. The test will pass whether CopyPassthroughRequestHeaders strips Proxy-Authorization or not.

Impact. No production bug exists. CopyPassthroughRequestHeaders correctly strips Proxy-Authorization via IsBrokerScopedRequestHeader, and this is verified at unit level by TestCopyPassthroughRequestHeaders_StripsBrokerScoped in brokercore_test.go, which explicitly calls src.Set("Proxy-Authorization", "Basic xxx") and asserts it is absent from dst. However, the integration test provides false confidence: a future regression removing Proxy-Authorization stripping from CopyPassthroughRequestHeaders would not be caught by this test.

Addressing the refutation. The refuting verifier correctly notes that (1) production code is correct and (2) unit-level coverage exists. Both points are valid and fully acknowledged here. This report is filed at nit severity precisely because there is no production defect — it is a test quality gap: a vacuous assertion that gives false confidence without exercising the actual stripping code path.

How to fix it. Add req.Header.Set("Proxy-Authorization", "Basic dW5yZWxhdGVk") to the inner request before client.Do(req), then keep the existing sawProxyAuth != "" assertion. With that change the test will actually exercise CopyPassthroughRequestHeaders rather than passing trivially.

Step-by-step proof. (1) newTrustingClient encodes url.User("av_sess_ok") into the proxy URL. (2) http.Transport sends CONNECT <host> HTTP/1.1 with Proxy-Authorization: Basic YXZfc2Vzc19vazA= — this is the CONNECT handshake credential. (3) The proxy handles CONNECT, validates the session, and returns 200 Connection Established. (4) Subsequent HTTP requests flow inside the encrypted TLS tunnel; http.Transport does NOT add Proxy-Authorization to these in-tunnel requests. (5) The upstream handler receives r.Header.Get("Proxy-Authorization") == "" always. (6) sawProxyAuth != "" is never true, so t.Fatalf is unreachable.

</details>

🟡 The JSON mode "Key fields" section in `cmd/skill_cli.md` is missing `passthrough` from the `services[].auth` type list. An agent using the CLI skill in JSON mode would see only four auth types and would not know `passthrough` is valid, potentially generating an invalid proposal or falling back to a credentialed type unnecessarily.

<details>
<summary>Extended reasoning...</summary>

**What the bug is and how it manifests:**

The PR adds a fifth auth type, `passthrough`, and correctly updates most of `cmd/skill_cli.md`: the auth-types code block (lines ~103–109), the passthrough explanatory paragraph, and the flag-driven auth flags list (line ~145). However, the JSON mode "Key fields" section immediately below was not updated. `skill_cli.md` line 151 still reads:

```
`services[].auth` -- authentication config. Types: `bearer` (`token`), `basic` (`username`, optional `password`), `api-key` (`key` + `header`, optional `prefix`), `custom` (`headers` map with `{{ KEY }}` templates)
```

**The specific code path that triggers it:**

When an agent uses `cmd/skill_cli.md` and reads the "Key fields (JSON mode)" section to understand what auth types are valid in a JSON proposal body, it sees four types, not five. The same line in `cmd/skill_http.md` was correctly updated to append `, `passthrough` (no credential fields)`.

**Why existing code does not prevent it:**

The diff shows `skill_http.md` was updated at the Key fields section, but the parallel edit was not applied to `skill_cli.md`. The `CLAUDE.md` convention requiring both files be updated together was only partially followed — the flag-driven and auth-table sections were synced, but the JSON mode prose section was missed.

**What the impact would be:**

An agent reading the CLI skill in JSON mode would not know `passthrough` is a valid `services[].auth` type. It might: (a) generate a proposal body without `passthrough` even when the operator wanted it, (b) invent a credential field unnecessarily, or (c) pick a credentialed auth type when passthrough was the correct choice. The omission makes the two skill files diverge, violating the versioned-pair invariant described in CLAUDE.md.

**How to fix it:**

Append `, `passthrough` (no credential fields)` to the `services[].auth` line in the JSON mode Key fields section of `cmd/skill_cli.md` (line ~151), matching the equivalent line in `cmd/skill_http.md`.

**Step-by-step proof:**

1. An agent is launched via `vault run` and loads `cmd/skill_cli.md`.
2. It needs to propose a new passthrough service and reads the "Key fields" section to understand the JSON shape.
3. The section lists four auth types with no mention of `passthrough`.
4. The agent either omits the service or picks `bearer`/`basic`/`api-key`/`custom`, forcing the operator to supply a credential that was never needed.
5. Had the agent used `cmd/skill_http.md` instead, it would have seen the correct five-type list and generated `{"type": "passthrough"}` with no credential fields.

</details>

🔴 The PR introduces a direct contradiction between the new "Making Requests" section and the unchanged Rules section in both skill files. Line 32 of skill_cli.md (line 31 of skill_http.md) now states that unconfigured/unauthenticated hosts "still pass through the proxy unmodified -- no special handling required," but the Rules section in both files still reads "**Only** request hosts returned by discover -- if a host isn't listed, create a proposal." An agent following the authoritative Rules section literally would refuse to call any unauthenticated public API not in /discover and would instead create unnecessary proposals, directly contradicting the new main-section framing. The Rules rule should be narrowed to credentialed/authenticated requests only, or updated to clarify that unconfigured hosts route through the transparent proxy without a proposal.

<details>
<summary>Extended reasoning...</summary>

**What the bug is and how it manifests**

Both skill files now describe two different behaviors for unauthenticated or unconfigured-host requests. The "Making Requests" and introductory sections (updated in this PR) say these requests "pass through the proxy unmodified -- no special handling required." But the Rules sections (not updated in this PR) still say "**Only** request hosts returned by discover -- if a host isn't listed, create a proposal." An AI agent reading both sections encounters an unresolvable contradiction, and since the Rules section is structured as the authoritative, distilled list of behavioral constraints, a strict agent would follow Rules over the prose.

**The specific code path that triggers it**

In skill_cli.md, the old line 32 said: "Unauthenticated requests or requests to services not configured in Agent Vault should be made directly." This was consistent with the Rules rule because "made directly" meant bypassing the proxy entirely -- so the Rule ("Only request hosts returned by discover") applied only to proxy-routed, credentialed requests. The PR changed line 32 to: "Unauthenticated requests or requests to hosts not configured in Agent Vault still pass through the proxy unmodified -- no special handling required." Now unconfigured hosts DO go through the proxy, but the Rules section still reads as an absolute prohibition on requesting any host not in /discover. The same pattern applies identically in skill_http.md (line 31 / Rules line ~246).

**Why existing code doesn't prevent it**

The Rules section in both files was not updated as part of this PR. The old wording in the Rules was internally consistent with the old behavior (bypass proxy for unconfigured hosts). The PR changed the mental model from "bypass if unconfigured" to "always route through proxy, just without credential injection," but only updated the prose sections, not the Rules bullet. There is no mechanism in a markdown skill file to enforce consistency across sections.

**What the impact would be**

An agent strictly following the Rules section would interpret "Only request hosts returned by discover" as an absolute prohibition on any HTTP request to a host not in /discover, including public unauthenticated APIs (e.g., a weather API, a public GitHub endpoint, an OpenStreetMap tile server). The agent would create a proposal for every such host, requiring human approval even for calls that need no credentials and should succeed transparently. This is the opposite of the intent expressed in the new "Making Requests" framing, which explicitly says "no special handling required" for such calls.

**How to fix it**

Narrow the Rules bullet to apply only to credentialed requests. For example, change:
- 

to:
- 

Or add a clarifying sub-bullet: 

The same fix applies in both skill_cli.md and skill_http.md.

**Step-by-step proof**

1. An agent is launched via `vault run` and needs to fetch public data from `api.openweathermap.org` without credentials.
2. Agent reads the workflow: step 4 says "If the host is NOT listed, create a proposal" -- this is about credentialed requests.
3. Agent runs `discover` and sees `api.openweathermap.org` is not in the services list.
4. Agent reads the new line 32 (skill_cli.md): "Unauthenticated requests or requests to hosts not configured in Agent Vault still pass through the proxy unmodified -- no special handling required." This suggests it can proceed directly.
5. Agent then reads the Rules section (line ~242): "**Only** request hosts returned by discover -- if a host isn't listed, create a proposal." This is phrased as an absolute rule with no carve-out for unauthenticated hosts.
6. Rules section contradicts step 4. A rule-following agent creates a proposal for `api.openweathermap.org`, presenting an unnecessary approval URL to the user for a completely public API.

</details>

body:
🔴 The new "Making Requests" section incorrectly claims that `fetch` and `axios` honor `HTTPS_PROXY` automatically — this is false for Node.js environments, where both require explicit proxy agent configuration. An agent writing Node.js code would follow the transparent-MITM path, silently bypass the proxy, and receive 401s from upstream APIs with no injected credentials.

<details>
<summary>Extended reasoning...</summary>

**What the bug is and how it manifests**

The sentence "Standard HTTP clients (curl, fetch, requests, axios, the Go stdlib, etc.) honor `HTTPS_PROXY` automatically" is factually incorrect for two of the listed clients when running in a Node.js environment. Node.js native fetch (Node 18+, undici-based) does NOT read `HTTPS_PROXY` from the environment by default — undici requires explicit `ProxyAgent`/`setGlobalDispatcher` configuration. Similarly, axios in Node.js relies on Node's `http`/`https` modules, which do not natively honour `HTTPS_PROXY`; proxy support in axios is version-dependent and not transparently reliable. The same incorrect claim appears in both `cmd/skill_cli.md` (the primary affected file at line 65) and `cmd/skill_http.md`.

**The specific code path that triggers it**

An agent reading this skill doc sees the primary workflow: "just call the real API URL" — `curl https://api.stripe.com/v1/charges` or `fetch('https://api.stripe.com/v1/charges')`. The doc says all of curl, fetch, requests, axios, and Go stdlib auto-honour `HTTPS_PROXY`, so an agent writing Node.js code will use native `fetch` or `axios` pointing at the real API host. Because `HTTPS_PROXY` is set in the environment (by `vault run`) but Node.js/undici ignores it, the request goes directly to the upstream without passing through the MITM proxy. No credential is injected.

**Why existing code doesn't prevent it**

The docs do acknowledge a fallback scenario: "The HTTP client doesn't honor `HTTPS_PROXY` (rare)". But listing fetch and axios in the very same section as clients that *do* honour it makes the fallback appear inapplicable to them. An agent following the docs has no reason to think it needs the explicit `/proxy/{host}/{path}` form when using `fetch` or `axios` — the docs explicitly told it those clients work transparently. The contradiction is internal to this PR's new text.

**Step-by-step proof**

1. `vault run` sets `HTTPS_PROXY=http://127.0.0.1:14322` and `NODE_EXTRA_CA_CERTS=/tmp/vault-ca.crt` in the child environment.
2. Agent reads the skill doc, sees `fetch` listed as an auto-proxy-honouring client.
3. Agent writes: `const resp = await fetch('https://api.stripe.com/v1/charges');`
4. Node.js 18+ uses undici for native fetch. undici does NOT read `HTTPS_PROXY`. It opens a direct TLS connection to `api.stripe.com:443`.
5. No MITM interception occurs. No credential is injected.
6. Stripe returns `401 Unauthorized` (or similar). The agent retries, checks discover, finds the host is configured, is confused.
7. The correct fix was to use the explicit proxy URL: `await fetch(`${process.env.AGENT_VAULT_ADDR}/proxy/api.stripe.com/v1/charges`, ...)` — which is exactly what the project README demonstrates for Node.js.

**What the impact is**

The failure is silent: no error indicates the proxy was bypassed, and the upstream 401 looks like a misconfigured credential rather than a missing proxy hop. This makes the bug hard to diagnose. The README already shows the correct Node.js fetch pattern (explicit `/proxy/` URL), which itself is evidence that transparent MITM does not work for Node.js fetch. The fallback section even describes the explicit-proxy path but characterises the need for it as "rare" — for Node.js, it's the *default* case.

**How to fix it**

Remove `fetch` and `axios` from the auto-honouring list, or add a qualification: "Standard HTTP clients (curl, Python requests, the Go stdlib, etc.) honor `HTTPS_PROXY` automatically. Node.js clients (native fetch / axios) typically require explicit proxy agent configuration — use the `/proxy/{host}/{path}` fallback form instead." This would align the doc with the README's own Node.js examples and prevent agents from silently bypassing credential injection.

</details>

🔴 The new "Making Requests" section states "Your code can leave the upstream auth header blank or set it to a placeholder — Agent Vault attaches the real credential at the proxy boundary," but this is incorrect for passthrough-configured services accessed via MITM. For passthrough services, the MITM path forwards the Authorization header unchanged to upstream, so a blank or placeholder value causes a 401. The passthrough section later documents this correctly, but the general guidance has no carve-out and will mislead agents following the primary path. The same inaccuracy exists in the identical text in cmd/skill_http.md:80.

<details>
<summary>Extended reasoning...</summary>

**What the bug is and how it manifests**

The new "Making Requests" section (skill_cli.md:65, skill_http.md:80) makes a universal claim: "Your code can leave the upstream auth header blank or set it to a placeholder — Agent Vault attaches the real credential at the proxy boundary." This is only true for credentialed auth types (bearer, basic, api-key, custom). For passthrough-configured services accessed via the MITM ingress, no credential is injected, and the client's Authorization header is forwarded verbatim to the upstream API. Sending a blank or placeholder Authorization to upstream causes a 401 Unauthorized.

**The specific code path that triggers it**

In internal/mitm/forward.go:68, the MITM path calls `brokercore.ApplyInjection(r.Header, outReq.Header, inject)` with no `extraStrip` arguments. For passthrough services (`inject.Passthrough == true`), ApplyInjection calls `CopyPassthroughRequestHeaders(src, dst)` with no extra strips. That function uses a denylist approach: it strips only hop-by-hop headers and broker-scoped headers (X-Vault, Proxy-Authorization). Authorization is NOT in either denylist, so it passes through to the upstream unchanged.

**Why existing code doesn't prevent it**

The explicit /proxy path (handle_proxy.go:199) passes "Authorization" as extraStrip: `ApplyInjection(r.Header, outReq.Header, inject, "Authorization")`. This correctly strips the Authorization header even for passthrough services. But the MITM path has no such strip. The passthrough section later in both documents correctly describes this per-ingress difference, but the general Making Requests section presents the placeholder advice as universally applicable without mentioning this important exception.

**What the impact would be**

An agent reading the primary "Making Requests" guidance and following it for a passthrough-configured service will set Authorization: Bearer placeholder (or leave it blank), route through MITM, and have that placeholder forwarded verbatim to the upstream API — resulting in a 401. This is a real authentication failure for a documented feature combination newly introduced as the primary workflow by this PR.

**How to fix it**

Add a carve-out in the Making Requests section noting that the blank/placeholder guidance applies only to credentialed auth types (bearer, basic, api-key, custom). For passthrough-configured services via MITM, agents must supply the real upstream Authorization header themselves. Something like: "(Note: for passthrough-configured services, Agent Vault does not inject credentials — your code must provide the real upstream Authorization header directly.)
**Step-by-step proof**

1. Operator configures api.example.com as passthrough (`auth.type = "passthrough"`), meaning they hold the credential and want audit coverage via MITM.
2. Agent reads the new "Making Requests" guidance and follows it: sets Authorization: Bearer placeholder in its HTTP client (or leaves it blank).
3. vault run is active, so the request routes through HTTPS_PROXY → MITM ingress.
4. MITM forward.go:68 calls ApplyInjection with no extraStrip.
5. inject.Passthrough == true, so CopyPassthroughRequestHeaders is called.
6. Authorization is not in the hop-by-hop or broker-scoped denylists, so Authorization: Bearer placeholder is copied to outReq.Header unchanged.
7. Upstream api.example.com receives Authorization: Bearer placeholder → returns 401 Unauthorized.
8. If the agent had instead used the explicit /proxy fallback, handle_proxy.go:199 would have passed "Authorization" as extraStrip, stripping the placeholder — but passthrough still wouldn't inject a real credential, so the request would proceed without Authorization (which may also fail, but for a different reason).

</details>

🟡 This PR reframes skill files to teach MITM-first, but README.md (lines 22, 106) and several docs/ pages still present explicit `/proxy/{host}/{path}` as the primary agent request pattern — creating a direct contradiction between agent-facing skill files and developer-facing documentation. A developer following README/docs would implement explicit-proxy agents while deployed agents using the updated skills would use MITM instead; CLAUDE.md lines 50-51 explicitly require updating README.md and docs/ when operator-facing behavior changes.

<details>
<summary>Extended reasoning...</summary>

**What the bug is and how it manifests**

This PR updates `cmd/skill_cli.md` and `cmd/skill_http.md` to reframe the primary agent request path from explicit `/proxy/{host}/{path}` to transparent MITM via `HTTPS_PROXY`. Before this PR, skill files, README.md, and docs/ were all consistent: explicit proxy was the taught primary path. After this PR, skill files say MITM is primary and explicit proxy is a fallback, but README.md and multiple docs/ files still present explicit proxy as the primary mechanism — creating a direct contradiction.

**The specific code path / files affected**

README.md line 22 still reads: 'Your agent gets a token and a proxy URL. It sends requests to `proxy/{host}/{path}`' — positioning explicit proxy as the core agent pattern. README.md line 106 shows a fetch example using `${vault}/proxy/api.github.com/user/repos`. `docs/agents/protocol.mdx` lines 84-101 say 'For hosts returned by /discover, the agent routes requests through the Agent Vault proxy: `{AGENT_VAULT_ADDR}/proxy/{host}/{path}`'. `docs/quickstart/custom-agent.mdx` and other docs/ pages provide only explicit-proxy code examples.

**Why existing code doesn't prevent it**

CLAUDE.md lines 50-51 explicitly require: 'When a change affects operator-facing behavior, update README.md' and 'Whenever a new feature lands, scan docs/ for pages that need a matching update — quickstart, guides, self-hosting, learn, and reference all mirror runtime behavior and drift fast.' The PR only touches the two skill files and does not update README.md or any docs/ files, violating these stated conventions.

**Addressing the refutation**

The refutation argues the README inconsistency predates this PR and that this is 'documentation-reframing' not a behavior change. This is partially correct — MITM existed since PRs #74/#75 — but misses the key point: *before* this PR, skill files and README/docs were *consistent* (all taught explicit-proxy-first). *After* this PR, they directly contradict each other. The PR introduces a new inconsistency by changing the skill-file framing without updating the documentation that developers use to implement agents. The refutation's 'may follow separately in a stacked PR' argument does not change the fact that this PR, as written, creates a contradiction.

**Impact**

A developer building a new agent by following README.md or any docs/ page would build an explicit-proxy agent. A deployed agent receiving the updated skill files would use MITM instead. These are opposite behaviors from the same project, causing potential integration failures and developer confusion.

**How to fix**

Update README.md lines 22 and 106 to lead with the MITM / real-URL pattern and demote explicit proxy to a fallback. Update `docs/agents/protocol.mdx`, `docs/quickstart/custom-agent.mdx`, `docs/agents/overview.mdx`, `docs/guides/connect-custom-agent.mdx`, and `docs/self-hosting/environment-variables.mdx` to mirror the MITM-first framing introduced in the skill files.

**Step-by-step proof**

1. Developer reads README.md line 22 today: 'It sends requests to `proxy/{host}/{path}`' → builds agent using `fetch(${AGENT_VAULT_ADDR}/proxy/api.github.com/user/repos)`
2. Agent is deployed via `vault run`, receives `skill_cli.md` v0.3.0 which says: 'Just call the real API URL... `curl https://api.github.com/user`'
3. Skill file explicitly labels explicit proxy 'Fallback: only when transparent MITM isn't viable'
4. Developer's agent is doing the 'fallback' thing the skill says to avoid; an agent following the skill would do the opposite of what the README says to do — direct contradiction from the same project documentation.

</details>

🟡 The 502 credential-not-found response embeds help links in the message string rather than a separate top-level help field, unlike the 403 response which correctly adds body.help. The PR description states both error paths now include a help field, but only the 403 path does — any agent or SDK that discovers help via body.help on a 403 will find nothing on a 502. Fix by using a structured body builder for the 502 case similar to ForbiddenHintBody.

<details>
<summary>Extended reasoning...</summary>

**What the bug is and how it manifests**

The PR introduces a helpLinks(baseURL) helper to surface actionable discovery URLs in broker-layer error responses. For the 403 (ErrServiceNotFound) path, ForbiddenHintBody correctly places the help text in a top-level "help" JSON key. For the 502 (ErrCredentialMissing) path, the same helpLinks output is appended to the message string in WriteInjectError, resulting in a flat {"error": "credential_not_found", "message": "A required credential...check vault configuration. To see available services, GET .../discover..."} with no separate help field.

**The specific code path that triggers it**

In internal/brokercore/brokercore.go, WriteInjectError for the ErrCredentialMissing case (lines ~210-220) builds a string via msg += ". " + helpLinks(baseURL) and passes it to WriteProxyError. WriteProxyError only serialises map[string]string{"error": code, "message": message} — there is no mechanism to emit additional top-level fields.

**Why existing code does not prevent it**

WriteProxyError uses a map[string]string body which cannot carry a separate help field without a signature change. ForbiddenHintBody uses map[string]interface{} precisely because it needs extra top-level fields. The 502 path reuses the simpler helper unchanged.

**What the impact would be**

Any agent, SDK, or tooling that reads body.help to extract actionable recovery URLs (a reasonable assumption given the PR explicitly describes adding that field to both paths) will receive nil/undefined on a 502 response and silently miss the help links. The inconsistency also contradicts the PR description, which states "502 (credential not found) proxy errors now include a help field with actionable URLs".

**How to fix it**

Either (a) change WriteProxyError to accept an optional extra fields map and populate help there, or (b) add a dedicated helper that builds a map[string]interface{} body analogous to ForbiddenHintBody and includes a top-level "help" key when baseURL is non-empty.

**Step-by-step proof**

1. Service api.example.com is configured in the vault but its credential key MY_KEY is absent from the store.
2. Agent routes GET https://api.example.com/resource through the MITM proxy.
3. Inject resolves the service but cannot find MY_KEY, returning ErrCredentialMissing.
4. WriteInjectError builds: msg = "A required credential could not be resolved; check vault configuration. To see available services, GET http://127.0.0.1:14321/discover..."
5. WriteProxyError(w, 502, "credential_not_found", msg) writes: {"error":"credential_not_found","message":"...GET http://127.0.0.1:14321/discover..."}
6. Agent parses body.help and gets undefined. The same agent on a 403 receives body.help = "This request was intercepted by Agent Vault. To see available services..." as a parseable string field.
7. Result: programmatic help-link discovery works on 403 but silently fails on 502, contradicting the stated design intent.

</details>
