🟡 The capability table at docs/learn/permissions.mdx:16 lists 'Manage agents (create, list, revoke, rotate, rename, set-role)' and the prose at line 123 claims 'Any authenticated user can create agents' — both clash with reality on this PR. The CLI verb is 'delete' (cmd/agent.go's `agentRevokeCmd` is `Use: "delete <name>"`) and server enforcement at internal/server/handle_agents.go:35 calls `requireInstanceMember`, which 403s for no-access actors. Fix: line 16 'revoke' → 'delete', and line 123 'Any authenticated user' → 'Any instance member' (which matches the table two paragraphs above).

<details>
<summary>Extended reasoning...</summary>

## What the bug is

This PR rewrote the agent-management language in `docs/learn/permissions.mdx` (the invite→create rename), and in doing so left two doc-prose inconsistencies on lines that were freshly touched. Both contradict the actual CLI/server surface in this same PR.

### 1. Line 16: `revoke` vs `delete`

The capability table reads:

> `| Manage agents (create, list, revoke, rotate, rename, set-role) | Yes | Yes | No |`

But the user-facing CLI verb is `delete`, not `revoke`. In `cmd/agent.go`:

```go
var agentRevokeCmd = &cobra.Command{
    Use:   "delete <name>",
    Short: "Delete an agent and all its tokens",
    ...
}
```

The Go identifier is still named `agentRevokeCmd` (because the underlying server endpoint is `handleAgentRevoke` and status='revoked'), but `Use: "delete <name>"` is what end users invoke. `docs/reference/cli.mdx` and `docs/agents/overview.mdx` all consistently use `delete`, and even the **same file** at line 123 reads:

> `agent-vault agent list`, `info`, `delete`, `rotate`, `rename`, and `set-role` are instance-level operations

So line 16 alone carries the stale `revoke` token — internally inconsistent with line 123 seven lines down and with the CLI/UI/cli.mdx surface everywhere else.

### 2. Line 123: 'Any authenticated user can create agents'

Two lines above this same paragraph, the table already shows the correct answer: `Manage agents (create, list, revoke, ...) | Yes | Yes | No` — No-Access = **No**. The prose at line 123 directly contradicts that and the server enforcement:

```go
// internal/server/handle_agents.go:35
func (s *Server) handleAgentCreate(w http.ResponseWriter, r *http.Request) {
    ctx := r.Context()
    actor, err := s.requireInstanceMember(w, r)
    if err != nil {
        return
    }
    ...
}
```

`requireInstanceMember` rejects no-access actors with 403 `Instance member role required`. Surrounding context corroborates: line 24 of this file calls out 'no creating other actors' as part of the no-access definition.

### Step-by-step proof

1. Operator reads the table at line 16, takes away that the CLI verb is 'revoke'.
2. Operator runs `agent-vault agent revoke my-agent` → Cobra error 'unknown command "revoke" for "agent-vault agent"'. Has to grep `agent-vault agent --help` to discover the verb is actually `delete`. (Or reads line 123 of the same doc and gets the correct answer.)
3. Separately, operator reads the prose at line 123 and concludes a no-access user can call `agent create`.
4. A no-access actor's POST /v1/agents hits `requireInstanceMember` → 403 'Instance member role required'. The CLI and table promised otherwise.

### Why existing code doesn't prevent it

The PR diff for this file shows lines 16 and 123 were both touched in this changeset (invite→create rename), so they had a window to be aligned. Lines 16/123 were edited without re-reading 'revoke' or the 'Any authenticated user' clause, so the rename landed but the surrounding stale wording rode along unchanged.

### Impact

Pure documentation quality — no functional impact. The CLI rejects 'revoke' fast and the server correctly enforces member+ on create, so the worst case is operator confusion and one wasted command. Worth aligning while the doc is fresh and these lines are being edited anyway.

### Fix

Two single-word edits:

- Line 16: `(create, list, revoke, rotate, rename, set-role)` → `(create, list, delete, rotate, rename, set-role)`
- Line 123: 'Any authenticated user can create agents' → 'Any instance member can create agents'

Both align the prose with the capability table immediately above and with the server-side ACL.

</details>

🟡 After creating an agent, the Connect Your Agent modal in `ConnectAgentView` at web/src/pages/home/AllAgentsTab.tsx:555-569 hardcodes `AGENT_VAULT_VAULT="<VAULT_NAME>"` even when the operator just picked a vault in the form — the `vaultAssignments` state from `AddAgentButton` (and the `vaults` array in the `/v1/agents` response) is dropped before reaching the snippet. The parallel CLI hint at cmd/agent_create.go:94-100 already does the right thing (pre-fill from `resp.Vaults[0].VaultName`, fall back to `<vault>` only when none assigned, note multi-vault). Thread `vaultAssignments` (or `createData.vaults`) into `ConnectAgentView` and mirror the CLI logic so an operator who picked `default:proxy` does not have to hand-edit the snippet that auto-filled TOKEN/ADDR for them.

<details>
<summary>Extended reasoning...</summary>

## What the bug is

`ConnectAgentView` at `web/src/pages/home/AllAgentsTab.tsx:555-569` accepts only `{ agentToken, baseURL }` as props and builds the env-var snippet for the modal as:

```ts
const envSnippet = [
  `export AGENT_VAULT_ADDR="${addr}"`,
  `export AGENT_VAULT_TOKEN="${agentToken}"`,
  `export AGENT_VAULT_VAULT="<VAULT_NAME>"`,
].join("\n");
```

The `<VAULT_NAME>` is a literal placeholder string, written unconditionally. Two values away — in the same file — the parent `AddAgentButton` already holds the picked vaults: `vaultAssignments` (line 253) and the `vaults` array echoed back in `createData` from `POST /v1/agents`. Neither is threaded into `ConnectAgentView` (the render site at line 408 is `<ConnectAgentView agentToken={createResult.agentToken} baseURL={baseURL} />`), so they are dropped on the floor.

## The CLI got this right

The matching CLI hint introduced by the same PR at `cmd/agent_create.go:94-100` does the smart thing:

```go
vaultHint := "<vault>"
if len(resp.Vaults) > 0 {
    vaultHint = resp.Vaults[0].VaultName
}
fmt.Fprintf(w, "  AGENT_VAULT_TOKEN=%q AGENT_VAULT_VAULT=%q agent-vault run -- <command>\n", resp.AvAgentToken, vaultHint)
if len(resp.Vaults) > 1 {
    fmt.Fprintf(w, "\n(Multiple vaults were pre-assigned; pick the vault this run should use ...)\n")
}
```

So `agent-vault agent create my-agent --vault default:proxy` prints `AGENT_VAULT_VAULT="default"`, while the UI in the same shipping commit prints `AGENT_VAULT_VAULT="<VAULT_NAME>"` for the identical operation. The data needed to do the right thing is one component-prop away.

## Step-by-step proof

1. Operator clicks **Add agent** in the All Agents tab, types `my-agent`, leaves Instance role at `no-access`, clicks **+ Add vault**, picks `default` with role `proxy`, and clicks **Add**.
2. `AddAgentButton.handleCreate` builds `payload = {name: "my-agent", role: "no-access", vaults: [{vault_name: "default", vault_role: "proxy"}]}` (lines 325-333) and POSTs to `/v1/agents`.
3. Server `handleAgentCreate` returns 201 with `{av_agent_token, name, role, vaults: [{vault_name: "default", vault_role: "proxy"}], created_at}` (internal/server/handle_agents.go:130-136).
4. `AddAgentButton` reads `createData.av_agent_token`, calls `setCreateResult({ agentToken: createData.av_agent_token })` — the `vaults` field of `createData` is dropped on the floor.
5. Render path swaps to `<ConnectAgentView agentToken={...} baseURL={...} />`. No vault information reaches the component.
6. `ConnectAgentView` renders the snippet pane. The operator copies:

   ```
   export AGENT_VAULT_ADDR="..."
   export AGENT_VAULT_TOKEN="av_agt_..."
   export AGENT_VAULT_VAULT="<VAULT_NAME>"
   ```

7. Pasting that into the agent host literally exports the placeholder string `<VAULT_NAME>`. Running `agent-vault run` against that env yields `403 No access to this vault` (no vault named `<VAULT_NAME>`), or if it survives, every proxy call carries the wrong `X-Vault` header.

The operator has to manually look up the vault they picked one screen earlier and edit the snippet they were about to paste — the exact friction the auto-filled TOKEN and ADDR slots were meant to eliminate.

## Why existing code does not prevent it

There is no existing code that would. The component was renamed in this PR (`InviteResultView` → `ConnectAgentView`) and its prop signature was preserved as-is; the `<VAULT_NAME>` placeholder was carried over from the invite-era snippet where the vault selection was less coupled to the connect flow. The parent simply was not updated to pass the new information through when the form picker matured. No test asserts on the snippet contents either.

## Impact

Severity is **nit** because:
- The placeholder is obviously a placeholder, so the failure mode is "operator notices and hand-edits" rather than "silent miswiring."
- An operator who pastes verbatim will get a fast, intelligible 403 the moment the agent makes a proxy call.
- No security implication — there is no upstream that will accept the literal string `<VAULT_NAME>` as a vault.

But it is a real CLI/UI consistency gap in the very flow this PR rewrites, and the fix is mechanical. The PR description claims the UI "shows the same connect-modal as before," but the surrounding code (form-driven vault picker, returned `vaults` payload) is now richer than the snippet exposes.

## Suggested fix

Thread the vault info one level down. Either of these works:

```tsx
// Option A: pass vaultAssignments from the form
setCreateResult({ agentToken: createData.av_agent_token, vaults: createData.vaults ?? vaultAssignments });
// ...
<ConnectAgentView
  agentToken={createResult.agentToken}
  baseURL={baseURL}
  vaults={createResult.vaults}
/>
```

Then in `ConnectAgentView`, mirror the CLI:

```tsx
const vaultHint = vaults && vaults.length > 0 ? vaults[0].vault_name : "<VAULT_NAME>";
const envSnippet = [
  `export AGENT_VAULT_ADDR="${addr}"`,
  `export AGENT_VAULT_TOKEN="${agentToken}"`,
  `export AGENT_VAULT_VAULT="${vaultHint}"`,
].join("\n");
// Optionally render a note when vaults.length > 1, paralleling the CLI's multi-vault hint.
```

Prefer `createData.vaults` (server-echoed) over `vaultAssignments` (form state) so the snippet always reflects what the server actually granted.

</details>

🟡 The security page's token table at docs/learn/security.mdx:70 still describes the agent-token TTL as `Configurable (or no expiry)`, but this PR removes the only API path that could set a finite TTL (the old invite flow's `session_ttl_seconds`). Both `handleAgentCreate` and `handleAgentRotate` now hard-code `nil` for the token expiry, and neither the `POST /v1/agents` request struct, `cmd/agent_create.go`, nor `cmd/agent.go` expose a TTL flag — so every agent token issued is now no-expiry. The cell should read `No expiry` (or the API should grow a `ttl_seconds` field on create/rotate) so the threat-model description matches reality.

<details>
<summary>Extended reasoning...</summary>

## Bug

`docs/learn/security.mdx:70` describes the agent-token row of the token table as:

```
| Agent token | `av_agt_` | SHA-256 | Configurable (or no expiry) | Instance-level agent identity |
```

`Configurable` was accurate pre-PR — the invite flow accepted `session_ttl_seconds`, which `handlePersistentInviteRedeem` threaded through to `CreateAgentToken` as a finite expiry. This PR deletes the invite ceremony and the only API surfaces that minted agent tokens (create + rotate) now hard-code `nil` for the expiry.

## The code paths that mint agent tokens

There are exactly two post-PR ways to obtain an agent token, and both pass `nil`:

1. **Create** — `internal/server/handle_agents.go:115`:
   ```go
   agent, sess, err := s.store.CreateAgentWithGrantsAndToken(
       ctx, req.Name, actor.ID, agentRole, grantSpecs, nil)
   //                                                  ^^^ tokenExpiresAt
   ```
   The `POST /v1/agents` request struct decoded above (`internal/server/handle_agents.go:44-48`) has only `Name`, `Role`, and `Vaults` — no `ttl` / `ttl_seconds` / `expires_at` field. There is no client-controlled knob.

2. **Rotate** — `internal/server/handle_agents.go:309`:
   ```go
   sess, err := s.store.RotateAgentToken(ctx, agent.ID, nil)
   //                                                   ^^^ tokenExpiresAt
   ```
   `handleAgentRotate` accepts no request body fields at all.

The CLI doesn't add a knob either:
- `cmd/agent_create.go` registers only `--vault`, `--role`, `--token-only`, `--address`.
- `cmd/agent.go`'s `agentRotateCmd` registers only `--token-only`.

A grep for `ttl`, `TTL`, or `expir` against `cmd/agent_create.go` and `cmd/agent.go` returns no matches.

## Step-by-step proof

1. Operator reads `docs/learn/security.mdx` to understand the threat model: row 70 promises that the agent-token TTL is `Configurable (or no expiry)`. They reasonably conclude that the API exposes a knob to bound an agent token's lifetime, e.g. for short-lived CI tokens.
2. Operator tries `agent-vault agent create my-bot --ttl 1h` — fails, no such flag.
3. Operator reads the API reference and sends `POST /v1/agents` with `{"name":"my-bot","ttl_seconds":3600}` — the struct decoder silently drops the unknown field; the agent is created with no expiry.
4. Operator queries `GET /v1/agents/my-bot` — `token_expires_at` is omitted (the handler at `internal/server/handle_agents.go:227-230` only populates it when `GetLatestAgentTokenExpiry` returns non-nil; with `nil` expiry the column is `NULL`).
5. The doc has misled the operator: there is no configurability, only "no expiry."

## Why this is a real (if small) issue

This is the same category of stale prose the PR's previous review pass fixed for `docs/agents/overview.mdx` (the "By default, agents are created with the `member` instance role" → `no-access` flip). `security.mdx` just wasn't touched. The PR's commit context did update the table two lines down — line 71 deletes the Invite row that this same change removed — so the row at line 70 is clearly in scope for the same sweep.

An operator using this page to assess threat-model exposure would over-estimate the controls available: knowing an agent token *can* be bounded changes how willing one is to issue a long-lived credential.

## How to fix

One of:

1. **Doc-only (trivial)**: change the cell at line 70 from `Configurable (or no expiry)` to `No expiry`. Matches reality exactly.
2. **API restore**: re-introduce a `ttl_seconds` field on the `POST /v1/agents` and `POST /v1/agents/{name}/rotate` request bodies (and corresponding `--ttl` flags on `cmd/agent_create.go` and `agentRotateCmd`), wire it through to the existing `tokenExpiresAt` parameter both store calls already accept. The store already supports finite expiry (`Session.ExpiresAt`); only the HTTP/CLI surface was lost.

Severity is **nit** — pure documentation drift, not a functional or security regression. The `or no expiry` half of the cell is still accurate; only the `Configurable` half is stale.

</details>

🟡 🟡 The one-liner suggested at `cmd/agent_create.go:99` only sets `AGENT_VAULT_TOKEN` and `AGENT_VAULT_VAULT` even though the prose two lines above names three required env vars (TOKEN, ADDR, VAULT). `resolveSession` at cmd/helpers.go:518-519 hard-errors when `AGENT_VAULT_TOKEN` is set but `AGENT_VAULT_ADDR` is empty ("both are required for agent mode"), so a literal copy-paste into a fresh remote shell — the exact scenario this hint targets — fails before exec. The `addr` variable is already resolved at cmd/agent_create.go:29-32; slot it in as `AGENT_VAULT_ADDR=%q` to match the prose. Same shape as the previously-flagged `AGENT_VAULT_VAULT` omission; the ADDR slot was just missed.

<details>
<summary>Extended reasoning...</summary>

## What the bug is

After `agent-vault agent create <name>`, the CLI prints (cmd/agent_create.go:98-99):

```
Set AGENT_VAULT_TOKEN, AGENT_VAULT_ADDR, and AGENT_VAULT_VAULT in the agent's environment, or run:
  AGENT_VAULT_TOKEN="..." AGENT_VAULT_VAULT="default" agent-vault run -- <command>
```

The prose names **three** env vars; the one-liner sets **two**. The missing one is `AGENT_VAULT_ADDR`. This is the same shape as the `AGENT_VAULT_VAULT` omission already flagged and fixed earlier in this PR cycle — the fix just missed the ADDR slot.

## Why the literal one-liner fails

`agent-vault run` re-enters its own process and calls `resolveSession()` at cmd/helpers.go:515-520:

```go
func resolveSession() (*session.ClientSession, string, error) {
    token := os.Getenv(envVarToken)
    addr := os.Getenv("AGENT_VAULT_ADDR")
    if token != "" && addr == "" {
        return nil, "", fmt.Errorf("%s is set but AGENT_VAULT_ADDR is empty — both are required for agent mode", envVarToken)
    }
    ...
}
```

The check fires *before* anything else: it short-circuits even before the env-token probe (`validateEnvToken`) or the exec of the child. So the agent never starts.

## Step-by-step proof

1. Operator runs `agent-vault agent create my-agent --vault default:proxy` on their workstation. They have a local session at `~/.agent-vault/session.json`, so `addr` resolves and the create succeeds.
2. CLI prints the hint, including the literal one-liner: `AGENT_VAULT_TOKEN="av_agt_..." AGENT_VAULT_VAULT="default" agent-vault run -- <command>`.
3. Operator SSHes to the remote host where the agent will actually run (a fresh CI runner, container shell, etc.). This host has no `~/.agent-vault/session.json` and no env vars preset — that is exactly the scenario the hint is targeting (the prose right above it explicitly says "in the agent's environment").
4. Operator pastes the one-liner, substitutes `<command>` with their agent binary, runs it.
5. `agent-vault run` starts, calls `resolveSession()`. `AGENT_VAULT_TOKEN` is set (from the pasted prefix), `AGENT_VAULT_ADDR` is unset (the env-var prefix never mentioned it). Line 518 fires.
6. Process exits with `AGENT_VAULT_TOKEN is set but AGENT_VAULT_ADDR is empty — both are required for agent mode` before the child is ever execd.

## Why existing code does not prevent it

The hint is generated only on the success path of agent-create — there is no validator that cross-checks the printed env vars against `resolveSession`'s requirements. The local workstation case (where the operator pastes the same line into the same shell they ran `agent create` from) succeeds *coincidentally* because that shell either inherited `AGENT_VAULT_ADDR` from `auth login` or picks it up from `session.json` — neither of which applies on the remote shell the hint is for. The CLI UI of `web/src/pages/home/AllAgentsTab.tsx` correctly shows three exports (`AGENT_VAULT_ADDR`, `AGENT_VAULT_TOKEN`, `AGENT_VAULT_VAULT`) in its `ConnectAgentView` snippet, which is the same pattern the CLI hint should match.

## Impact

Severity **nit**: the error message from `resolveSession` is reasonably clear, so operators recover quickly by exporting `AGENT_VAULT_ADDR`. But the literal copy-paste path that the hint advertises does not work as printed in its target scenario (a fresh remote shell). Worth fixing in this PR while `agent_create.go` is still new — same one-line shape as the VAULT fix that already landed for this comment thread.

## Fix

`addr` is already resolved at cmd/agent_create.go:29-32. Add it to the printf:

```go
fmt.Fprintf(w, "  AGENT_VAULT_TOKEN=%q AGENT_VAULT_ADDR=%q AGENT_VAULT_VAULT=%q agent-vault run -- <command>\n", resp.AvAgentToken, addr, vaultHint)
```

</details>

🟡 The bullet list at docs/guides/connect-custom-agent.mdx:36-39 still advertises an `av_addr` field in the `POST /v1/agents` response, but the new `handleAgentCreate` at internal/server/handle_agents.go:126-132 only returns `{av_agent_token, name, role, vaults, created_at}`. Drop the `av_addr` bullet (the doc one section down already tells operators to set `AGENT_VAULT_ADDR` from their own config), or replace it with the actual fields (`name`, `role`, `created_at`) so an integrator parsing the JSON does not get `undefined`.

<details>
<summary>Extended reasoning...</summary>

## What the bug is

The "agent create" tab of `docs/guides/connect-custom-agent.mdx` (lines 36-39) lists three fields it claims the create response includes:

```
- `av_addr` — the Agent Vault server URL
- `av_agent_token` — bearer token for all requests
- `vaults` — list of accessible vaults
```

This is a holdover from the deleted invite-redeem response, which did emit `av_addr` (built from `s.baseURL`). The PR rewrote the surrounding prose for the invite→create rename ("redeems it via POST {invite_url} and receives" became "Prints the agents token (copies to clipboard). The response also includes") but carried the bullet list over verbatim.

## The actual response shape

The new `handleAgentCreate` at `internal/server/handle_agents.go:126-132` writes exactly five fields:

```go
jsonCreated(w, map[string]interface{}{
    "av_agent_token": sess.ID,
    "name":           agent.Name,
    "role":           agent.Role,
    "vaults":         vaultInfos,
    "created_at":     agent.CreatedAt.Format(time.RFC3339),
})
```

No `av_addr`. The two extra fields (`name`, `role`, `created_at`) the doc does not mention.

## Step-by-step proof

1. Integrator follows the doc and runs `curl -X POST http://localhost:14321/v1/agents -H "Authorization: Bearer $SESS" -d {"name":"my-agent","vaults":[{"vault_name":"default","vault_role":"proxy"}]}`.
2. Server returns 201 with body `{"av_agent_token":"av_agt_...","name":"my-agent","role":"no-access","vaults":[{"vault_name":"default","vault_role":"proxy"}],"created_at":"2026-05-15T..."}`.
3. Integrator parses the JSON expecting `av_addr` per the doc — gets `undefined`/`null` and has to read source (or the working CLI handler at `cmd/agent_create.go:62-72`) to discover the field never existed in the new shape.

## Impact

Pure documentation drift — no functional or security regression. An integrator notices on the first `JSON.parse` and works around it. The doc one paragraph down (line 41) already tells operators to "Set `AGENT_VAULT_TOKEN` and `AGENT_VAULT_ADDR` in the agents runtime", so the address is meant to come from the operators own config, not from the API response.

## How to fix

One-line doc edit at lines 36-39:

```diff
-Prints the agents token (copies to clipboard). The response also includes:
-- `av_addr` — the Agent Vault server URL
-- `av_agent_token` — bearer token for all requests
-- `vaults` — list of accessible vaults
+Prints the agents token (copies to clipboard). The response also includes:
+- `av_agent_token` — bearer token for all requests
+- `name`, `role`, `created_at` — the agent identity the server persisted
+- `vaults` — list of accessible vaults
```

Severity **nit** — same category as the other doc-drift items already flagged on this PR (overview.mdx default-role, security.mdx TTL cell). Worth fixing in the same surface area the PR rewrote.

</details>

+---
+title: "Tutorial"
+description: "Walk through your first vault, service, and agent end to end."
+---
+
+import InstallCommand from "/snippets/install-command.mdx";
+
+This tutorial takes you from a freshly deployed Agent Vault instance to a Claude Code session making authenticated calls through Agent Vault. Agent Vault and Claude Code should run on two different machines on the same private network.
+
+By the end, you'll have:
+
+1. An Agent Vault instance set up with credentials and credential brokering rules for the services your agent needs to reach.
+2. A Claude Code agent proxying its requests through Agent Vault, making authenticated requests to GitHub without holding any real credentials. This, by the way, works with any other agent ([OpenCode](/quickstart/opencode), [OpenClaw](/quickstart/openclaw), [Hermes Agent](/quickstart/hermes-agent), [custom agents](/quickstart/custom-agent), etc.) and even traditional deterministic workloads.
+
+## Prerequisites
+
+- An Agent Vault server [installed](/installation) and running on a **separate host** from where the agent will run, and reachable over the same network.
+- An API key to broker for Claude Code. This tutorial uses a [GitHub personal access token (PAT)](https://github.com/settings/tokens), invoked via the [GitHub CLI](https://cli.github.com/), but this could be any credential and tool combination.
+
+Steps 1–5 all happen in the Agent Vault web UI at `http://<your-host>:14321`. Step 6 runs the agent on the agent host.
+
+## 1. Register the instance owner
+
+Open `http://<your-host>:14321/register` in a browser and create your account. The first user to register becomes the instance [owner](/learn/permissions#instance-roles) and is auto-granted admin on the `default` [vault](/learn/vaults).
+
+![Create Owner Account registration page](/images/tutorial/tutorial-register.png)
+
+After registering, you land in the dashboard signed in as the owner.
+
+## 2. Create a vault
+
+A [vault](/learn/vaults) is the logical container for credentials, services, and the agents allowed to use them. The `default` vault is fine for testing, but we'll create a dedicated one to mirror real usage.
+
+In the sidebar, open **Vaults** and click **New vault**. Name it `claude-code` and create it.
+
+![New vault dialog with name claude-code](/images/tutorial/tutorial-create-vault.png)
+
+## 3. Add a credential
+
+Open the `claude-code` vault and go to the **[Credentials](/learn/credentials)** tab. Click **Add credential** and enter:
+
+- **Key**: `GITHUB_TOKEN`
+- **Value**: your GitHub PAT (`ghp_...`)
+
+![Add Credential form with key GITHUB_TOKEN](/images/tutorial/tutorial-add-credential.png)
+
+## 4. Define a service
+
+A [service](/learn/services) tells Agent Vault which upstream host the agent can reach and how to wire the credential in. For this tutorial we'll use the **passthrough + substitution** pattern: Agent Vault doesn't pick an auth header for you, it just swaps a placeholder string the agent sends for the real credential.
+
+In the same vault, go to the **Services** tab, click **Add service**, and enter:
+
+- **Name**: `github`
+- **Host**: `api.github.com`
+- **Auth type**: `passthrough`
+- **Substitution**:
+  - **Key**: `GITHUB_TOKEN`
+  - **Placeholder**: `__github_token__`
+  - **In**: `header`

<details>
<summary>Extended reasoning...</summary>

### What goes wrong

The Substitution bullets in `docs/tutorial.mdx:56-59` describe the form as if it had three labeled fields:

```
- **Key**: `GITHUB_TOKEN`
- **Placeholder**: `__github_token__`
- **In**: `header`
```

The actual UI at `web/src/pages/vault/ServicesTab.tsx:751-810` is rendered as an inline prose sentence:

> Replace `[__placeholder__]` in `[path]` `[query]` `[header]` with value of `[CREDENTIAL_KEY]`

There is no field literally labeled **Key**, **Placeholder**, or **In** — the placeholder/key are inline `<InlineInput>`s and the surfaces are three `role="switch"` toggle buttons rendered by mapping over `SUBSTITUTION_SURFACES` (lines 764-799).

### Why the default makes it functionally broken (not just cosmetic)

A newly added substitution row is initialized with `in: [...DEFAULT_SUBSTITUTION_SURFACES]` at `ServicesTab.tsx:822`, and `DEFAULT_SUBSTITUTION_SURFACES` is `["path", "query"]` at `web/src/components/ProposalPreview.tsx:23`. So the header surface is **off** by default.

A reader following the tutorial verbatim will hunt for an "In" field, fail to find one, and — assuming "In: header" is either a no-op or already implied — fill in only the key and placeholder. They save a substitution whose `in` is `["path", "query"]`.

### Step-by-step proof the tutorial fails

1. Tutorial step 6 sets `GH_TOKEN="__github_token__"` and runs `agent-vault run -- claude`.
2. The user asks Claude Code to list their repos via `gh`. The `gh` CLI takes `GH_TOKEN` from the environment and puts it in the `Authorization: Bearer __github_token__` request **header** when calling `https://api.github.com/...`.
3. The MITM proxy matches the request against the `github` service. It iterates the configured substitutions; this one has `in = ["path", "query"]`, so it scans the URL path and query string for `__github_token__`. The placeholder isn't in either — it's in the Authorization header.\n4. The request is forwarded upstream with the literal string `__github_token__` still in the Authorization header.\n5. GitHub rejects it with `401 Unauthorized`, `gh` errors out, and Claude Code reports failure. The tutorial's headline end-to-end demo — the whole point of the page — silently does not work.\n\n### Why existing prose doesn't save the reader\n\nThe screenshot `tutorial-define-service.png` might show the right toggle state, but the bullet list immediately above is the authoritative instruction in a tutorial format. The list never tells the reader that `path` and `query` are on by default and need to be turned **off**, nor that `header` needs to be turned **on** — readers treating the bullets as a checklist will miss it.\n\n### Suggested fix\n\nReplace the three-bullet Substitution block with something that describes the actual sentence-style editor, e.g.:\n\n```markdown\n- **Substitution**: Fill the substitution row so it reads:\n  > Replace `__github_token__` in **header** with value of `GITHUB_TOKEN`\n\n  The surfaces row defaults to `path` + `query` selected — click **path** and **query** to deselect them, then click **header** to select it.\n```\n\nThis matches both the UI labels (or lack thereof) and corrects the default-surface gotcha in one stroke.

</details>

🟡 The **Connect more agents** card at lines 113-115 describes "Cursor, Codex, OpenCode, and custom runtimes" but links to `/quickstart/claude-code` — the agent the reader just finished setting up. Consider either retargeting the href (e.g. `/quickstart/custom-agent`) or reframing the title/description so it matches the Claude Code page the link actually goes to.

<details>
<summary>Extended reasoning...</summary>

**What the bug is.** On the new tutorial page, the *Next steps* section ends with a four-card grid. The first card reads:

```mdx
<Card title="Connect more agents" icon="robot" href="/quickstart/claude-code">
  Cursor, Codex, OpenCode, and custom runtimes.
</Card>
```

The title (*Connect more agents*) and the body (which explicitly enumerates Cursor, Codex, OpenCode, and custom runtimes — and notably **omits** Claude Code) promise a hub or menu of *other* agents. The href, however, drops the reader on `/quickstart/claude-code`, the single-agent Claude Code quickstart they just finished walking through in this very tutorial.

**Why existing structure doesn't paper over it.** `docs.json` defines a redirect `/quickstart` → `/quickstart/claude-code`, so there is no true hub page to link to. Mintlify's sidebar does surface the full Quickstart group when the user lands on `/quickstart/claude-code` (cursor, codex, openclaw, hermes-agent, opencode, custom-agent), so discovery via the sidebar still works in principle. That mitigates the impact but doesn't resolve the textual mismatch — the card promises content the destination page does not deliver, and the user must notice the sidebar on their own.

**Step-by-step proof.** (1) Reader follows the tutorial through step 7, completing a Claude Code + GitHub flow. (2) Reader reaches *Next steps* and reads the first card: "Connect more agents — Cursor, Codex, OpenCode, and custom runtimes." (3) Reader clicks expecting a menu of alternative agents. (4) Browser navigates to `/quickstart/claude-code`, which renders the Claude Code-specific page (verified: `docs/quickstart/claude-code.mdx` is Claude-Code-only). (5) Reader sees the page for the very agent they just set up — none of Cursor, Codex, OpenCode, or custom runtimes is visible above the fold; they live only in the left sidebar.

**Addressing the refutation.** A similar pattern does exist in `docs/installation.mdx:65` ("Connect an agent" → `/quickstart/claude-code` with body "Setup guides for Claude Code, Cursor, Codex, and more."). That makes this consistent with prior convention, but two things distinguish the tutorial case: (a) the installation card *includes* Claude Code in its description, while the tutorial card explicitly *omits* it — so the mismatch is sharper here; (b) the tutorial reader has just spent the page setting up Claude Code, so being routed back to it is more jarring than for a reader arriving from the install page. The refutation's point that no real hub exists is correct, but that's an argument for reframing the card text, not for keeping a mismatched link.

**How to fix.** Easiest fix: rephrase the card so it matches the destination, e.g. title "More on Claude Code" or description "Claude Code quickstart and other agents." Alternative: retarget the href to `/quickstart/custom-agent` (which is the closest thing to a generic entry point) and keep the existing copy. Lowest-risk: change the description to "Claude Code, Cursor, Codex, OpenCode, and more." so it no longer reads as *only* other agents.

</details>

<details>

```mdx
{/* TODO image: screenshot of the post-create screen showing the AGENT_VAULT_ADDR / AGENT_VAULT_TOKEN / AGENT_VAULT_VAULT export block */}
```

It sits between step 5 ("Create an agent") and step 6 ("Run Claude Code through Agent Vault"). The author flagged their own work as unfinished.

**Why this matters even though Mintlify hides MDX comments**

MDX strips `{/* ... */}` from rendered HTML, so a reader on the docs site will never see the TODO text. The bug is not the comment string — it's what the comment is marking. The prose immediately above on line 71 promises:

> After creating the agent, Agent Vault shows a ready-to-copy block of the three env vars you'll need on the agent host. **Copy it; the token is only displayed this once.**

That is precisely the moment a screenshot is most useful: the user gets one chance to copy the token, the screen has a specific layout, and step 6 then asks them to "paste the block from step 5". Yet step 5 is the only step in the walkthrough with no image. Steps 1 (register), 2 (create vault), 3 (add credential), 4 (define service), the agent-create form, and step 7 (logs) all have inline screenshots — the absence at step 5 is structurally conspicuous, not a stylistic choice.

+---
+title: "Run Hermes on a VPS"
+description: "Keep real credentials off the agent host by routing every outbound call through Agent Vault on a separate VPS."
+---
+
+Provision two Hetzner VPS boxes, install Agent Vault on one and Hermes Agent on the other, and broker every outbound call through Agent Vault. Plan for 60–90 minutes and ~€10/month.
+
+By the end, you'll have:
+
+1. **Agent Vault running on one VPS**, holding real Anthropic, GitHub, Slack, and Telegram credentials encrypted at rest behind a master password.
+2. **A [Hermes Agent](https://github.com/NousResearch/hermes-agent) running on a second VPS**, reachable via a Telegram bot, with every outbound API call brokered through Agent Vault and revocable from the UI in one click.
+
+{/* TODO(jake): swap YOUTUBE_VIDEO_ID for the real ID once the video is published. */}
+<iframe
+  width="100%"
+  height="450"
+  src="https://www.youtube.com/embed/YOUTUBE_VIDEO_ID"
+  title="Run Hermes on a VPS: companion video"
+  frameborder="0"
+  allow="accelerometer; autoplay; clipboard-write; encrypted-media; gyroscope; picture-in-picture; web-share"
+  referrerpolicy="strict-origin-when-cross-origin"
+  allowfullscreen
+></iframe>
+
+## Prerequisites
+
+- A [Hetzner Cloud](https://www.hetzner.com/cloud) account.
+- API keys for the services you want Hermes to call. This guide uses Anthropic, GitHub, and Slack.
+- A Telegram account on your phone.
+
+<Note>
+This guide installs Agent Vault as a native binary via the install script, the path documented in [Self-hosting locally](/self-hosting/local). For containers, see [Docker self-hosting](/self-hosting/docker).
+</Note>
+
+## Architecture
+
+```
++-----------------------------------------------------------------+
+| Public internet                                                 |
+|                                                                 |
+|   api.anthropic.com   api.github.com                            |
+|   slack.com           api.telegram.org                          |
+|          ^                   ^                                  |
++----------+-------------------+----------------------------------+
+           |                   |
+           +-------------------+
+                               | outbound HTTPS, Agent Vault
+                               | injects real credentials here
++------------------------------+----------------------------------+
+| Private network (av-net, 10.0.0.0/24)                           |
+|                              |                                  |
+|  +---------------------------+----+     +--------------------+  |
+|  | av-broker  10.0.0.2            |     | hermes-vps         |  |
+|  | Agent Vault server             |<----| 10.0.0.3           |  |
+|  | :14321  control UI / API       |     | Hermes Agent +     |  |

+|  | (real credentials, encrypted)  |     | (placeholders)     |  |
+|  +----------------^---------------+     +--------------------+  |
+|                   |                                             |
++-------------------+---------------------------------------------+
+                    | SSH + tunnel for AV UI from laptop
+                    | (browser admin; phone for Telegram bot)
+                    |
+                Operator
+```
+
+Only `av-broker` holds real credentials, encrypted at rest behind your master password. `hermes-vps` holds placeholder strings (`__anthropic_api_key__`, etc.) and one revocable [agent token](/agents/overview).
+
+## 1. Provision the VPS boxes
+
+<Steps>
+
+<Step title="Create a Hetzner project">
+
+In the [Hetzner Cloud Console](https://console.hetzner.cloud), click **+ New Project**. Name it (e.g. `agent-vault-lab`) and click in. Everything that follows happens inside this project.
+
+</Step>
+
+<Step title="Generate an SSH key on your laptop">
+
+```bash
+ssh-keygen -t ed25519 -f ~/.ssh/agent-vault-lab -C "agent-vault-lab"
+```
+
+Every `ssh` command in this guide uses `-i ~/.ssh/agent-vault-lab` to pin to this key.
+
+</Step>
+
+<Step title="Upload the public key to Hetzner">
+
+In the project sidebar: **Security → SSH Keys → Add SSH Key.** Paste the contents of `~/.ssh/agent-vault-lab.pub`, name it (e.g. `lab`), and tick **Make default for this project** before saving.

+</Step>
+
+<Step title="Create the private network">

+**Networks → Create Network.** Set:

+<Step title="Create and attach the firewall">
+
+**Firewalls → Create Firewall**, name `ssh-lockdown`. Add one inbound rule:
+
+- **Protocol:** TCP
+- **Port:** `22`
+- **Source IPs:** the IPv4 from the previous step
+
+Leave outbound rules empty (Hetzner allows all outbound by default).
+
+After saving, scroll down to **Apply To → Servers** and tick both `av-broker` and `hermes-vps`.
+
+</Step>
+
+</Steps>
+
+<Warning>
+If your laptop's public IP changes (cafe networks, VPNs), update the firewall rule's source IP.
+</Warning>
+
+## 3. Install Agent Vault on av-broker
+
+<Steps>
+
+<Step title="SSH into av-broker">
+
+From your laptop:
+
+```bash
+ssh -i ~/.ssh/agent-vault-lab root@<av-broker-public-ip>
+```
+
+Every command in this phase runs on `av-broker` until you exit.
+
+</Step>
+
+<Step title="Install Agent Vault">
+
+```bash
+curl --proto '=https' --proto-redir '=https' --tlsv1.2 -fsSL https://get.agent-vault.dev | sh
+```
+
+The script detects your architecture, verifies the signed release, and drops the binary at `/usr/local/bin/agent-vault`.
+
+</Step>
+
+<Step title="Install tmux">
+
+```bash
+apt update && apt install -y tmux
+```
+
+You'll run Agent Vault inside a `tmux` session so it survives your SSH disconnect.
+
+</Step>
+
+<Step title="Launch the server inside tmux">
+
+```bash
+tmux new -s av
+agent-vault server --host 10.0.0.2 --port 14321 --mitm-port 14322
+```
+
+`--host 10.0.0.2` binds both listeners to the private NIC, keeping Agent Vault unreachable from the public internet.
+
+First-run prompts: master password, admin email, admin password.
+
+Detach with `Ctrl-B` then `D`. You'll see `[detached from session av]` and drop back to your normal shell. The server keeps running inside the tmux session.
+
+</Step>
+
+<Step title="Verify the server">
+
+```bash
+curl -sI http://10.0.0.2:14321/health
+```
+
+Expect `HTTP/1.1 200 OK`.
+
+</Step>
+
+</Steps>
+
+<Note>
+On reboot, tmux dies and so does the server. SSH back in, `tmux new -s av`, restart with the same command, re-enter the master password. For zero-touch restart, set [`AGENT_VAULT_MASTER_PASSWORD`](/self-hosting/environment-variables), but note the password then lives in an env file.
+</Note>
+
+## 4. Configure the vault
+
+<Steps>
+
+<Step title="Open an SSH tunnel">
+
+In a **new terminal on your laptop** (don't reuse the one you used to install Agent Vault):
+
+```bash
+ssh -i ~/.ssh/agent-vault-lab -L 14321:10.0.0.2:14321 root@<av-broker-public-ip> -N
+```
+
+The terminal hangs silently. That's correct. **Leave it running for the rest of the guide.** Closing it stops the tunnel and the AV UI goes dark.
+
+Open `http://localhost:14321` in your laptop's browser and sign in with the admin email and password you set during install.
+
+</Step>
+
+<Step title="Understand vaults, credentials, and services">
+
+You'll create one of each. Briefly:
+
+- A [**vault**](/learn/vaults) is a named isolation boundary. We'll create `prod`.
+- A [**credential**](/learn/credentials) is one secret value stored under a name (e.g. `ANTHROPIC_API_KEY = sk-ant-...`). Encrypted at rest.
+- A [**service**](/learn/services) is the wiring for one upstream host: host pattern + auth mode + substitution rules that reference credentials by name.
+
+Credentials store values. Services define wiring. At request time, Agent Vault matches the service by host, looks up the named credential, and rewrites the wire bytes before forwarding.
+
+</Step>
+
+<Step title="Create the prod vault">
+
+**Vaults → New vault → `prod` → Create.**
+
+</Step>
+
+<Step title="Add credentials">
+
+In the `prod` vault, **Credentials tab → Add credential.** This guide configures four credentials; Anthropic (model) and Telegram (inbound channel) are required for the rest of the guide to work, the others are illustrative. Substitute or add credentials for whatever services you want Hermes to call.
+
+| Key | Value |
+| --- | --- |
+| `ANTHROPIC_API_KEY` | Anthropic API key (`sk-ant-...`) |
+| `GITHUB_TOKEN` | GitHub PAT with `repo` scope |
+| `SLACK_BOT_TOKEN` | Slack bot token (`xoxb-...`) |
+| `TELEGRAM_BOT_TOKEN` | Placeholder; you create the real bot in the next section |
+
+If you're using Slack, the bot needs `chat:write`, `channels:read`, and `groups:read` scopes. Reinstall the app after adding them so the token picks them up, and invite the bot to your target channel.
+
+</Step>
+
+<Step title="Add services">
+
+**Services tab → + Add service.** For each row below: fill **Name** and **Host**, set **Authentication** to **Passthrough**, then scroll to **URL Substitutions** and click **+ Add substitution**. Paste the placeholder, tick exactly one **Surface** box (untick the others), select the credential. Save.
+
+Each substitution rule tells Agent Vault to scan that surface in outbound requests for the placeholder string and swap it for the credential's value before forwarding. Hermes emits placeholders on the wire; the real keys never leave `av-broker`.
+
+| Name | Host | Placeholder | Surface | Credential |
+| --- | --- | --- | --- | --- |
+| `anthropic-brain` | `api.anthropic.com` | `__anthropic_api_key__` | `header` | `ANTHROPIC_API_KEY` |
+| `github` | `api.github.com` | `__github_token__` | `header` | `GITHUB_TOKEN` |
+| `slack` | `slack.com/*` | `__slack_bot_token__` | `header` | `SLACK_BOT_TOKEN` |
+| `telegram` | `api.telegram.org` | `__telegram_bot_token__` | **`path`** | `TELEGRAM_BOT_TOKEN` |
+
+Three services use `header` (the upstream reads the credential from an HTTP header). Telegram uses `path` because its Bot API encodes the token inline in the URL (`/bot<TOKEN>/sendMessage`).
+
+</Step>
+
+</Steps>
+
+<Warning>
+**Placeholder strings are exact-match.** If an upstream returns 401, check the failing request's **Credential keys** field in the AV UI's **Logs** tab; an empty value means the substitution didn't fire.
+</Warning>
+
+## 5. Create the Telegram bot
+
+<Steps>
+
+<Step title="Mint the bot via BotFather">
+
+In Telegram, message `@BotFather`. Send `/newbot`, give it a display name, then a username ending in `bot`. BotFather returns a token: `123456789:ABC-DEF...`.
+
+</Step>
+
+<Step title="Paste the real token into Agent Vault">
+
+In the AV UI: `prod` → **Credentials** → `TELEGRAM_BOT_TOKEN` → edit → paste the BotFather token → save.
+
+</Step>
+
+<Step title="Get your numeric Telegram user ID">
+
+Message `@userinfobot`, send `/start`. Copy the numeric `Id:` value.
+
+</Step>
+
+</Steps>
+
+## 6. Connect Hermes
+
+<Steps>
+
+<Step title="SSH into hermes-vps and install the Agent Vault CLI">
+
+In a **fresh terminal on your laptop** (leave the SSH tunnel to `av-broker` running):
+
+```bash
+ssh -i ~/.ssh/agent-vault-lab root@<hermes-vps-public-ip>
+curl --proto '=https' --proto-redir '=https' --tlsv1.2 -fsSL https://get.agent-vault.dev | sh
+```
+
+Every command from here through starting the gateway runs on `hermes-vps`. On this box the AV CLI is a client wrapper; no server runs here.
+
+</Step>
+
+<Step title="Install Hermes and walk the setup wizard">
+
+```bash
+curl -fsSL https://raw.githubusercontent.com/NousResearch/hermes-agent/main/scripts/install.sh | bash
+```
+
+The install script drops Hermes at `/usr/local/lib/hermes-agent/` and then launches an interactive four-question setup wizard. Answer:
+
+1. **How would you like to set up Hermes?** → **Quick setup**.
+
+![Hermes first-launch setup: Quick setup vs Full setup](/images/hermes-on-vps/hermes-on-vps-wizard-setup.png)
+
+2. **Select provider:** scroll to the bottom and choose **Leave unchanged**.
+
+![Hermes provider list with Leave unchanged selected at the bottom](/images/hermes-on-vps/hermes-on-vps-wizard-provider.png)
+
+3. **Select terminal backend:** **Keep current (local)**.
+
+![Hermes terminal backend list with Keep current local selected](/images/hermes-on-vps/hermes-on-vps-wizard-terminal.png)
+
+4. **Connect a messaging platform?** **Skip** (set up later via `hermes setup gateway`). You'll configure Telegram in a later section using the gateway wizard.
+
+![Hermes messaging platform prompt with Skip selected](/images/hermes-on-vps/hermes-on-vps-wizard-messaging.png)
+
+The wizard exits and you're back at the shell prompt.
+
+</Step>
+
+<Step title="Write placeholder credential lines into Hermes's .env">
+
+```bash
+cat > ~/.hermes/.env <<'EOF'
+ANTHROPIC_API_KEY=__anthropic_api_key__
+GITHUB_TOKEN=__github_token__
+SLACK_BOT_TOKEN=__slack_bot_token__
+TELEGRAM_BOT_TOKEN=__telegram_bot_token__
+EOF
+```
+
+These placeholders match the substitution rules you created earlier.
+
+</Step>
+
+<Step title="Mint an agent token (back to your laptop's AV UI)">
+
+Switch to the AV UI tab in your laptop browser. Sidebar: **All Agents → Add agent.**
+
+- **Agent name:** `hermes-vps`
+- **Vault access:** click **+ Add vault**, pick `prod`, leave role at `proxy`
+- Click **Add**
+
+The modal flips to the **Connect Your Agent** view with a copyable snippet of three `export` lines. Broker address and agent token are pre-filled; the vault name is a placeholder. Click the inline **Copy** button. You'll paste it in the next step.
body:
🔴 The prose in the 'Mint an agent token' step has the pre-filled fields inverted: with this guide's setup the broker address renders as the placeholder `<AGENT_VAULT_ADDR>` (because `agent-vault server` is launched without `AGENT_VAULT_ADDR` set, so `/v1/status` omits `base_url` and `resolveAgentVaultAddr` returns the placeholder), while the vault name is pre-filled as `prod` (because the user has already attached the vault, so `vaultHint` uses `vaults[0].vault_name`). The follow-up 'Export the three AV env vars' step compounds this by showing a literal `http://10.0.0.2:14321` (which the user did not copy) and telling them to replace `<VAULT_NAME>` (which is not in the snippet). Invert the prose so it matches what the UI actually emits — and update the follow-up snippet to swap the real placeholder, `<AGENT_VAULT_ADDR>`, for `http://10.0.0.2:14321`.

<details>
<summary>Extended reasoning...</summary>

## What the bug is

Lines 408–410 of `docs/guides/hermes-on-vps.mdx` describe the AV UI's Connect Agent snippet as:

> Broker address and agent token are pre-filled; the vault name is a placeholder.

This is exactly backwards for the setup the guide walks through. The UI will render the broker address as a placeholder (`<AGENT_VAULT_ADDR>`) and the vault name as the literal string `prod`. Lines 419–425 then show a hand-written snippet with a literal `http://10.0.0.2:14321` and instruct the user to "Replace `<VAULT_NAME>` with `prod`" — but `<VAULT_NAME>` will not appear in what they pasted, while the real placeholder that *does* need replacing (`<AGENT_VAULT_ADDR>`) goes unmentioned.

## Why the UI behaves this way

**Broker address (placeholder, not pre-filled).** `internal/server/handle_spa.go:24` only exposes `base_url` in `/v1/status` when the operator has explicitly set the `AGENT_VAULT_ADDR` env var:

```go
if os.Getenv("AGENT_VAULT_ADDR") != "" {
    resp["base_url"] = s.BaseURL()
}
```

Section 3 of this guide launches `agent-vault server --host 10.0.0.2 --port 14321 --mitm-port 14322` inside tmux with no env wiring, so `base_url` is absent from the status response. On the client, `resolveAgentVaultAddr` (`web/src/pages/home/AllAgentsTab.tsx:537–555`) treats undefined as the placeholder string:

```ts
function resolveAgentVaultAddr(baseURL?: string): string {
  const placeholder = "<AGENT_VAULT_ADDR>";
  if (!baseURL) return placeholder;
  ...
}
```

So the snippet's first line renders `export AGENT_VAULT_ADDR="<AGENT_VAULT_ADDR>"`.

**Vault name (pre-filled, not a placeholder).** `vaultHint` at `AllAgentsTab.tsx:570` uses `vaults[0].vault_name` whenever a vault is attached:

```ts
const vaultHint = vaults.length > 0 ? vaults[0].vault_name : "<VAULT_NAME>";
```

The guide's step 'Mint an agent token' tells the user to click '+ Add vault → `prod`' *before* clicking Add, so `vaults.length > 0` by the time the modal flips to the Connect view. The third line renders `export AGENT_VAULT_VAULT="prod"`.

## Step-by-step proof a user will hit this

1. User runs `agent-vault server --host 10.0.0.2 --port 14321 --mitm-port 14322` (guide §3) with no `AGENT_VAULT_ADDR` env. Server starts, `baseURL` is derived from `--host`/`--port` but **only** `resolveBaseURL` knows; `handleStatus` doesn't expose it.
2. User opens the SSH-tunneled UI at `http://localhost:14321`, hits `/v1/status` — response has no `base_url` field.
3. User goes to **All Agents → Add agent**, types `hermes-vps`, attaches the `prod` vault, clicks Add.
4. `ConnectAgentView` renders with `baseURL = undefined` and `vaults = [{ vault_name: "prod", ... }]`.
5. Snippet rendered to the user:

   ```bash
   export AGENT_VAULT_ADDR="<AGENT_VAULT_ADDR>"
   export AGENT_VAULT_TOKEN="<long-token-from-UI>"
   export AGENT_VAULT_VAULT="prod"
   ```

6. Guide tells them "Broker address … pre-filled; vault name is a placeholder" — wrong on both fields.
7. Guide's next step shows a different snippet with a literal `http://10.0.0.2:14321` and instructs replacing `<VAULT_NAME>` — but the user pasted a buffer where `AGENT_VAULT_ADDR` is still `<AGENT_VAULT_ADDR>` and `AGENT_VAULT_VAULT` is already `prod`. A careful reader is confused; a reader who pastes verbatim ends up with a broken `AGENT_VAULT_ADDR`.

## How to fix

In §6 'Mint an agent token', invert the prose, e.g.:

> The agent token and the vault name are pre-filled; the broker address is a placeholder. Click the inline **Copy** button. You'll fix the address in the next step.

In §6 'Export the three AV env vars', either (a) leave the literal-host snippet but change the instruction to "Replace `<AGENT_VAULT_ADDR>` with `http://10.0.0.2:14321`", or (b) tell the user to set `AGENT_VAULT_ADDR=http://10.0.0.2:14321` on the av-broker server side so the field arrives pre-filled (this would also require documenting that env in §3). Option (a) is the smallest change.

</details>

+2. **A [Hermes Agent](https://github.com/NousResearch/hermes-agent) running on a second VPS**, reachable via a Telegram bot, with every outbound API call brokered through Agent Vault and revocable from the UI in one click.

body:
🔴 The iframe `src` on lines 13–22 is literally `https://www.youtube.com/embed/YOUTUBE_VIDEO_ID` — a placeholder string, not a real video ID. The MDX comment on line 13 is a non-blocking TODO that does nothing at build/render time, so merging as-is publishes a 'Video unavailable' embed at the top of the guide until someone manually swaps the ID. Either gate the merge on the real video ID, or delete the iframe block (lines 13–22) and re-land it in a follow-up once the companion video ships.

<details>
<summary>Extended reasoning...</summary>

**What the bug is**

Lines 13–22 of `docs/guides/hermes-on-vps.mdx` embed a YouTube iframe whose `src` attribute is the literal string `https://www.youtube.com/embed/YOUTUBE_VIDEO_ID`. `YOUTUBE_VIDEO_ID` is a placeholder, not a real 11-character YouTube video identifier. The preceding MDX comment `{/* TODO(jake): swap YOUTUBE_VIDEO_ID for the real ID once the video is published. */}` documents that the author knows the value is wrong, but MDX comments are inert at render time — they are stripped by the compiler and do not gate, hide, or fail the build.

**How it manifests**

When Mintlify builds the docs site, the iframe element renders verbatim into the published HTML. A visitor loading `/guides/hermes-on-vps` will see, at the very top of the guide (right under the two-bullet 'By the end, you'll have' list), an iframe pointing at `https://www.youtube.com/embed/YOUTUBE_VIDEO_ID`. YouTube responds to that URL with its standard 'Video unavailable' frame, because no video with the ID `YOUTUBE_VIDEO_ID` exists. This is the first interactive element on the page — it is unmissable.

**Why existing code doesn't prevent it**

There is no build-time guard. The PR description itself states 'Companion to an upcoming YouTube video,' confirming the real ID does not yet exist at merge time. CI runs `make test` (per the PR checklist) but no link-checker or video-existence check is configured for this MDX page. Nothing else in the diff (e.g. `docs/docs.json`) catches the placeholder. The TODO comment is the only signal, and it is invisible to the build pipeline.

**Step-by-step proof**

1. Reviewer merges PR #179 as-is.
2. Mintlify rebuilds the docs site, compiling `hermes-on-vps.mdx` to HTML.
3. The MDX compiler strips `{/* TODO(jake): ... */}` (JSX comments do not appear in output) but preserves the JSX `<iframe>` element verbatim, including its `src` attribute.
4. Published HTML at `/guides/hermes-on-vps` contains `<iframe ... src="https://www.youtube.com/embed/YOUTUBE_VIDEO_ID" ...></iframe>`.
5. A user loads the page. The browser issues a GET to `https://www.youtube.com/embed/YOUTUBE_VIDEO_ID`.
6. YouTube has no video with ID `YOUTUBE_VIDEO_ID` and returns its standard embed-error response — a black 450px-tall frame reading 'Video unavailable. This video isn't available anymore.'
7. The user sees a broken video at the top of an otherwise polished guide, before any of the prose content.

**Impact**

User-visible defect on a brand-new published guide. The broken embed is the first thing a visitor sees on the page, undermining the guide's credibility before the actual content begins. No functional or security impact — the rest of the page works fine — but the regression is on the most prominent element of the document.

**How to fix**

Three reasonable options, in order of preference:

1. **Block the merge** on the real video ID — swap `YOUTUBE_VIDEO_ID` for the actual 11-char ID once the companion video is published.
2. **Delete lines 13–22** (the TODO comment and the entire iframe block) and re-land the embed in a follow-up PR once the video URL is known.
3. **Gate the iframe** behind a build-time check or feature flag, but this is overkill for a docs PR — option 2 is simpler.

</details>

+
+{/* TODO(jake): swap YOUTUBE_VIDEO_ID for the real ID once the video is published. */}
+<iframe

+
+## Prerequisites
+
+- A [Hetzner Cloud](https://www.hetzner.com/cloud) account.
+- API keys for the services you want Hermes to call. This guide uses Anthropic, GitHub, and Slack.
+- A Telegram account on your phone.
+
+<Note>
+This guide installs Agent Vault as a native binary via the install script, the path documented in [Self-hosting locally](/self-hosting/local). For containers, see [Docker self-hosting](/self-hosting/docker).
+</Note>
+
+## Architecture
+
+```
++-----------------------------------------------------------------+
+| Public internet                                                 |
+|                                                                 |
+|   api.anthropic.com   api.github.com                            |
+|   slack.com           api.telegram.org                          |
+|          ^                   ^                                  |
++----------+-------------------+----------------------------------+
+           |                   |
+           +-------------------+
+                               | outbound HTTPS, Agent Vault
+                               | injects real credentials here
++------------------------------+----------------------------------+
+| Private network (av-net, 10.0.0.0/24)                           |
+|                              |                                  |
+|  +---------------------------+----+     +--------------------+  |
+|  | av-broker  10.0.0.2            |     | hermes-vps         |  |
+|  | Agent Vault server             |<----| 10.0.0.3           |  |
+|  | :14321  control UI / API       |     | Hermes Agent +     |  |
+|  | :14322  MITM proxy             |     | gateway daemon     |  |
+|  | (real credentials, encrypted)  |     | (placeholders)     |  |
+|  +----------------^---------------+     +--------------------+  |
+|                   |                                             |
++-------------------+---------------------------------------------+
+                    | SSH + tunnel for AV UI from laptop
+                    | (browser admin; phone for Telegram bot)
+                    |
+                Operator
+```
+
+Only `av-broker` holds real credentials, encrypted at rest behind your master password. `hermes-vps` holds placeholder strings (`__anthropic_api_key__`, etc.) and one revocable [agent token](/agents/overview).
+
+## 1. Provision the VPS boxes
+
+<Steps>
+
+<Step title="Create a Hetzner project">
+
+In the [Hetzner Cloud Console](https://console.hetzner.cloud), click **+ New Project**. Name it (e.g. `agent-vault-lab`) and click in. Everything that follows happens inside this project.
+
+</Step>
+
+<Step title="Generate an SSH key on your laptop">
+
+```bash
+ssh-keygen -t ed25519 -f ~/.ssh/agent-vault-lab -C "agent-vault-lab"
+```
+
+Every `ssh` command in this guide uses `-i ~/.ssh/agent-vault-lab` to pin to this key.
+
+</Step>
+
+<Step title="Upload the public key to Hetzner">
+
+In the project sidebar: **Security → SSH Keys → Add SSH Key.** Paste the contents of `~/.ssh/agent-vault-lab.pub`, name it (e.g. `lab`), and tick **Make default for this project** before saving.
+
+</Step>
+
+<Step title="Create the private network">
+
+**Networks → Create Network.** Set:
+
+- **Name:** `av-net`
+- **IP range:** `10.0.0.0/24`
+- **Network zone:** any (e.g. `eu-central`)
+
+</Step>
+
+<Step title="Create av-broker">
+
+**Servers → + Add Server.** Set:
+
+| Panel | Setting |
+| --- | --- |
+| **Location** | A datacenter in your `av-net` network zone (e.g. `nbg1`) |
+| **Image** | Ubuntu 24.04 |
+| **Type** | `CX23` (or any cheap x86 tier) |
+| **Networking** | Tick `av-net` under **Private networks**, then set the IP to `10.0.0.2` |
+| **Name** | `av-broker` |
+
+Click **Create & Buy now**.
+
+</Step>
+
+<Step title="Create hermes-vps">
+
+Repeat the previous step with two changes:
+
+- **Networking → Private network IP:** `10.0.0.3`
+- **Name:** `hermes-vps`
+
+</Step>
+
+<Step title="Verify private connectivity">
+
+From your laptop:
+
+```bash
+ssh -i ~/.ssh/agent-vault-lab root@<av-broker-public-ip>
+ping -c 3 10.0.0.3
+```
+
+Three replies confirms the private subnet is live. Type `exit` to disconnect.
+
+</Step>
+
+</Steps>
+
+## 2. Restrict SSH to your laptop
+
+<Steps>
+
+<Step title="Find your laptop's public IPv4">
+
+```bash

🟡 Inside the same wizard step, the guide references the gateway-setup command two different ways: line 379 says "set up later via `hermes setup gateway`" while line 449 runs `agent-vault run -- hermes gateway setup`. Only one subcommand order can be the real Hermes CLI invocation, so a reader who follows the line 379 hint will hit an "unknown command" error — reconcile both references to the single canonical form (and ideally wrap the line 379 hint in `agent-vault run --` so egress stays brokered).

<details>
<summary>Extended reasoning...</summary>

**What the bug is.** docs/guides/hermes-on-vps.mdx contains two contradictory references to the Hermes gateway setup wizard within the same step block.

At line 379 (inside step 4 of the Hermes setup wizard in section 6):
```
4. **Connect a messaging platform?** **Skip** (set up later via `hermes setup gateway`). You'll configure Telegram in a later section using the gateway wizard.
```

At line 449 (section 7, "Configure the Hermes gateway", under "Launch the wizard"):
```bash
agent-vault run -- hermes gateway setup
```

These are two different subcommand orderings — `setup gateway` vs `gateway setup` — for what the prose explicitly describes as the same wizard ("You'll configure Telegram in a later section using the gateway wizard" on line 379 points forward to section 7, where line 449 lives).

**Why this is a real bug.** A CLI cannot accept both forms transparently; at most one is the canonical command name. A reader who reads line 379 in passing and tries to run the gateway wizard later by typing what they remember (`hermes setup gateway`) will hit `unknown command` / `unknown subcommand`. Even the reader who follows the guide linearly will notice the discrepancy on reaching line 449 and may not know which form is authoritative.

**Step-by-step proof.**
1. Reader reaches section 6 step 4 of the wizard, picks **Skip**, and reads the parenthetical: *"set up later via `hermes setup gateway`"*. They mentally bookmark `hermes setup gateway` as the command to re-run later.
2. Reader later wants to configure Telegram and recalls the parenthetical. They run `hermes setup gateway` (or `agent-vault run -- hermes setup gateway`).
3. The Hermes CLI rejects this because the canonical subcommand path used in section 7 is `hermes gateway setup`, not `hermes setup gateway` (or vice versa). The reader gets an error and has to flip back to section 7 to find the actual command shown on line 449.

**Secondary issue (mentioned in the synthesis).** The line 379 hint is bare (`hermes setup gateway`), not wrapped in `agent-vault run --`. By section 8 the guide has gone to lengths to wire `HTTPS_PROXY` etc. into systemd, but at the moment of line 379 the gateway wizard would still need the brokered environment to talk to its dependencies; section 7 deliberately uses `agent-vault run --` for exactly this reason. The hint on line 379 should match.

**Suggested fix.** Pick the canonical form (whichever the Hermes CLI actually exposes — section 7's `hermes gateway setup` is the one written as an actual shell command and is therefore the more likely-to-be-correct form) and update line 379 to read, e.g.:

> 4. **Connect a messaging platform?** **Skip** (set up later via `agent-vault run -- hermes gateway setup`). You'll configure Telegram in a later section using the gateway wizard.

That single change fixes the contradiction and matches the broker-wrapping convention used elsewhere in the guide.

</details>

+<Step title="Install Hermes and walk the setup wizard">
+
+```bash
+curl -fsSL https://raw.githubusercontent.com/NousResearch/hermes-agent/main/scripts/install.sh | bash
+```
+
+The install script drops Hermes at `/usr/local/lib/hermes-agent/` and then launches an interactive four-question setup wizard. Answer:
+
+1. **How would you like to set up Hermes?** → **Quick setup**.
+
+![Hermes first-launch setup: Quick setup vs Full setup](/images/hermes-on-vps/hermes-on-vps-wizard-setup.png)
+
+2. **Select provider:** scroll to the bottom and choose **Leave unchanged**.
+
+![Hermes provider list with Leave unchanged selected at the bottom](/images/hermes-on-vps/hermes-on-vps-wizard-provider.png)
+
+3. **Select terminal backend:** **Keep current (local)**.
+
+![Hermes terminal backend list with Keep current local selected](/images/hermes-on-vps/hermes-on-vps-wizard-terminal.png)
+
+4. **Connect a messaging platform?** **Skip** (set up later via `hermes setup gateway`). You'll configure Telegram in a later section using the gateway wizard.
+
+![Hermes messaging platform prompt with Skip selected](/images/hermes-on-vps/hermes-on-vps-wizard-messaging.png)
+
+The wizard exits and you're back at the shell prompt.
+
+</Step>
+
+<Step title="Write placeholder credential lines into Hermes's .env">
+
+```bash
+cat > ~/.hermes/.env <<'EOF'
+ANTHROPIC_API_KEY=__anthropic_api_key__
+GITHUB_TOKEN=__github_token__
+SLACK_BOT_TOKEN=__slack_bot_token__
+TELEGRAM_BOT_TOKEN=__telegram_bot_token__
+EOF
+```
+
+These placeholders match the substitution rules you created earlier.
+
+</Step>
+
+<Step title="Mint an agent token (back to your laptop's AV UI)">
+
+Switch to the AV UI tab in your laptop browser. Sidebar: **All Agents → Add agent.**
+
+- **Agent name:** `hermes-vps`
+- **Vault access:** click **+ Add vault**, pick `prod`, leave role at `proxy`
+- Click **Add**
+
+The modal flips to the **Connect Your Agent** view with a copyable snippet of three `export` lines. Broker address and agent token are pre-filled; the vault name is a placeholder. Click the inline **Copy** button. You'll paste it in the next step.

+## Prerequisites
+
+- A [Hetzner Cloud](https://www.hetzner.com/cloud) account.
+- API keys for the services you want Hermes to call. This guide uses Anthropic, GitHub, and Slack.
+- A Telegram account on your phone.
+
+<Note>
+This guide installs Agent Vault as a native binary via the install script, the path documented in [Self-hosting locally](/self-hosting/local). For containers, see [Docker self-hosting](/self-hosting/docker).
+</Note>
+
+## Architecture
+
+```
++-----------------------------------------------------------------+
+| Public internet                                                 |
+|                                                                 |
+|   api.anthropic.com   api.github.com                            |
+|   slack.com           api.telegram.org                          |
+|          ^                   ^                                  |
++----------+-------------------+----------------------------------+
+           |                   |
+           +-------------------+
+                               | outbound HTTPS, Agent Vault
+                               | injects real credentials here
++------------------------------+----------------------------------+
+| Private network (av-net, 10.0.0.0/24)                           |
+|                              |                                  |
+|  +---------------------------+----+     +--------------------+  |
+|  | av-broker  10.0.0.2            |     | hermes-vps         |  |
+|  | Agent Vault server             |<----| 10.0.0.3           |  |
+|  | :14321  control UI / API       |     | Hermes Agent +     |  |
+|  | :14322  MITM proxy             |     | gateway daemon     |  |
+|  | (real credentials, encrypted)  |     | (placeholders)     |  |
+|  +----------------^---------------+     +--------------------+  |
+|                   |                                             |
++-------------------+---------------------------------------------+
+                    | SSH + tunnel for AV UI from laptop
+                    | (browser admin; phone for Telegram bot)
+                    |
+                Operator
+```
+
+Only `av-broker` holds real credentials, encrypted at rest behind your master password. `hermes-vps` holds placeholder strings (`__anthropic_api_key__`, etc.) and one revocable [agent token](/agents/overview).
+
+## 1. Provision the VPS boxes
+
+<Steps>
+
+<Step title="Create a Hetzner project">
+
+In the [Hetzner Cloud Console](https://console.hetzner.cloud), click **+ New Project**. Name it (e.g. `agent-vault-lab`) and click in. Everything that follows happens inside this project.
+
+</Step>
+
+<Step title="Generate an SSH key on your laptop">
+
+```bash
+ssh-keygen -t ed25519 -f ~/.ssh/agent-vault-lab -C "agent-vault-lab"
+```
+
+Every `ssh` command in this guide uses `-i ~/.ssh/agent-vault-lab` to pin to this key.
+
+</Step>
+
+<Step title="Upload the public key to Hetzner">
+
+In the project sidebar: **Security → SSH Keys → Add SSH Key.** Paste the contents of `~/.ssh/agent-vault-lab.pub`, name it (e.g. `lab`), and tick **Make default for this project** before saving.
+
+</Step>
+
+<Step title="Create the private network">
+
+**Networks → Create Network.** Set:
+
+- **Name:** `av-net`
+- **IP range:** `10.0.0.0/24`
+- **Network zone:** any (e.g. `eu-central`)
+
+</Step>
+
+<Step title="Create av-broker">
+
+**Servers → + Add Server.** Set:
+
+| Panel | Setting |
+| --- | --- |
+| **Location** | A datacenter in your `av-net` network zone (e.g. `nbg1`) |
+| **Image** | Ubuntu 24.04 |
+| **Type** | `CX23` (or any cheap x86 tier) |
+| **Networking** | Tick `av-net` under **Private networks**, then set the IP to `10.0.0.2` |
+| **Name** | `av-broker` |
+
+Click **Create & Buy now**.
+
+</Step>
+
+<Step title="Create hermes-vps">
+
+Repeat the previous step with two changes:
+
+- **Networking → Private network IP:** `10.0.0.3`
+- **Name:** `hermes-vps`
+
+</Step>
+
+<Step title="Verify private connectivity">
+
+From your laptop:
+
+```bash
+ssh -i ~/.ssh/agent-vault-lab root@<av-broker-public-ip>
+ping -c 3 10.0.0.3
+```
+
+Three replies confirms the private subnet is live. Type `exit` to disconnect.
+
+</Step>
+
+</Steps>
+
+## 2. Restrict SSH to your laptop
+
+<Steps>
+
+<Step title="Find your laptop's public IPv4">
+
+```bash
+curl -4 ifconfig.me; echo
+```
+
+</Step>
+
+<Step title="Create and attach the firewall">
+
+**Firewalls → Create Firewall**, name `ssh-lockdown`. Add one inbound rule:
+
+- **Protocol:** TCP
+- **Port:** `22`
+- **Source IPs:** the IPv4 from the previous step
+
+Leave outbound rules empty (Hetzner allows all outbound by default).
+
+After saving, scroll down to **Apply To → Servers** and tick both `av-broker` and `hermes-vps`.
+
+</Step>
+
+</Steps>
+
+<Warning>
+If your laptop's public IP changes (cafe networks, VPNs), update the firewall rule's source IP.
+</Warning>
+
+## 3. Install Agent Vault on av-broker
+
+<Steps>
+
+<Step title="SSH into av-broker">
+
+From your laptop:
+
+```bash
+ssh -i ~/.ssh/agent-vault-lab root@<av-broker-public-ip>
+```
+
+Every command in this phase runs on `av-broker` until you exit.
+
+</Step>
+
+<Step title="Install Agent Vault">
+
+```bash
+curl --proto '=https' --proto-redir '=https' --tlsv1.2 -fsSL https://get.agent-vault.dev | sh
+```
+
+The script detects your architecture, verifies the signed release, and drops the binary at `/usr/local/bin/agent-vault`.
+
+</Step>
+
+<Step title="Install tmux">
+
+```bash
+apt update && apt install -y tmux
+```
+
+You'll run Agent Vault inside a `tmux` session so it survives your SSH disconnect.
+
+</Step>
+
+<Step title="Launch the server inside tmux">
+
+```bash
+tmux new -s av
+agent-vault server --host 10.0.0.2 --port 14321 --mitm-port 14322
+```
+
+`--host 10.0.0.2` binds both listeners to the private NIC, keeping Agent Vault unreachable from the public internet.
+
+First-run prompts: master password, admin email, admin password.
+
+Detach with `Ctrl-B` then `D`. You'll see `[detached from session av]` and drop back to your normal shell. The server keeps running inside the tmux session.
+
+</Step>
+
+<Step title="Verify the server">
+
+```bash
+curl -sI http://10.0.0.2:14321/health
+```
+
+Expect `HTTP/1.1 200 OK`.
+
+</Step>
+
+</Steps>
+
+<Note>
+On reboot, tmux dies and so does the server. SSH back in, `tmux new -s av`, restart with the same command, re-enter the master password. For zero-touch restart, set [`AGENT_VAULT_MASTER_PASSWORD`](/self-hosting/environment-variables), but note the password then lives in an env file.
+</Note>
+
+## 4. Configure the vault
+
+<Steps>
+
+<Step title="Open an SSH tunnel">
+
+In a **new terminal on your laptop** (don't reuse the one you used to install Agent Vault):
+
+```bash
+ssh -i ~/.ssh/agent-vault-lab -L 14321:10.0.0.2:14321 root@<av-broker-public-ip> -N
+```
+
+The terminal hangs silently. That's correct. **Leave it running for the rest of the guide.** Closing it stops the tunnel and the AV UI goes dark.
+
+Open `http://localhost:14321` in your laptop's browser and sign in with the admin email and password you set during install.
+
+</Step>
+
+<Step title="Understand vaults, credentials, and services">
+
+You'll create one of each. Briefly:
+
+- A [**vault**](/learn/vaults) is a named isolation boundary. We'll create `prod`.
+- A [**credential**](/learn/credentials) is one secret value stored under a name (e.g. `ANTHROPIC_API_KEY = sk-ant-...`). Encrypted at rest.
+- A [**service**](/learn/services) is the wiring for one upstream host: host pattern + auth mode + substitution rules that reference credentials by name.
+
+Credentials store values. Services define wiring. At request time, Agent Vault matches the service by host, looks up the named credential, and rewrites the wire bytes before forwarding.
+
+</Step>
+
+<Step title="Create the prod vault">
+
+**Vaults → New vault → `prod` → Create.**
+
+</Step>
+
+<Step title="Add credentials">
+
+In the `prod` vault, **Credentials tab → Add credential.** This guide configures four credentials; Anthropic (model) and Telegram (inbound channel) are required for the rest of the guide to work, the others are illustrative. Substitute or add credentials for whatever services you want Hermes to call.
+
+| Key | Value |
+| --- | --- |
+| `ANTHROPIC_API_KEY` | Anthropic API key (`sk-ant-...`) |
+| `GITHUB_TOKEN` | GitHub PAT with `repo` scope |
+| `SLACK_BOT_TOKEN` | Slack bot token (`xoxb-...`) |
+| `TELEGRAM_BOT_TOKEN` | Placeholder; you create the real bot in the next section |
+
+If you're using Slack, the bot needs `chat:write`, `channels:read`, and `groups:read` scopes. Reinstall the app after adding them so the token picks them up, and invite the bot to your target channel.
+
+</Step>
+
+<Step title="Add services">
+
+**Services tab → + Add service.** For each row below: fill **Name** and **Host**, set **Authentication** to **Passthrough**, then scroll to **URL Substitutions** and click **+ Add substitution**. Paste the placeholder, tick exactly one **Surface** box (untick the others), select the credential. Save.
+
+Each substitution rule tells Agent Vault to scan that surface in outbound requests for the placeholder string and swap it for the credential's value before forwarding. Hermes emits placeholders on the wire; the real keys never leave `av-broker`.
+
+| Name | Host | Placeholder | Surface | Credential |
+| --- | --- | --- | --- | --- |
+| `anthropic-brain` | `api.anthropic.com` | `__anthropic_api_key__` | `header` | `ANTHROPIC_API_KEY` |
+| `github` | `api.github.com` | `__github_token__` | `header` | `GITHUB_TOKEN` |
+| `slack` | `slack.com/*` | `__slack_bot_token__` | `header` | `SLACK_BOT_TOKEN` |
+| `telegram` | `api.telegram.org` | `__telegram_bot_token__` | **`path`** | `TELEGRAM_BOT_TOKEN` |
+
+Three services use `header` (the upstream reads the credential from an HTTP header). Telegram uses `path` because its Bot API encodes the token inline in the URL (`/bot<TOKEN>/sendMessage`).
+
+</Step>
+
+</Steps>
+
+<Warning>
+**Placeholder strings are exact-match.** If an upstream returns 401, check the failing request's **Credential keys** field in the AV UI's **Logs** tab; an empty value means the substitution didn't fire.
+</Warning>
+
+## 5. Create the Telegram bot
+
+<Steps>
+
+<Step title="Mint the bot via BotFather">
+
+In Telegram, message `@BotFather`. Send `/newbot`, give it a display name, then a username ending in `bot`. BotFather returns a token: `123456789:ABC-DEF...`.
+
+</Step>
+
+<Step title="Paste the real token into Agent Vault">
+
+In the AV UI: `prod` → **Credentials** → `TELEGRAM_BOT_TOKEN` → edit → paste the BotFather token → save.
+
+</Step>
+
+<Step title="Get your numeric Telegram user ID">
+
+Message `@userinfobot`, send `/start`. Copy the numeric `Id:` value.
+
+</Step>
+
+</Steps>
+
+## 6. Connect Hermes
+
+<Steps>
+
+<Step title="SSH into hermes-vps and install the Agent Vault CLI">
+
+In a **fresh terminal on your laptop** (leave the SSH tunnel to `av-broker` running):
+
+```bash
+ssh -i ~/.ssh/agent-vault-lab root@<hermes-vps-public-ip>
+curl --proto '=https' --proto-redir '=https' --tlsv1.2 -fsSL https://get.agent-vault.dev | sh
+```
+
+Every command from here through starting the gateway runs on `hermes-vps`. On this box the AV CLI is a client wrapper; no server runs here.
+
+</Step>
+
+<Step title="Install Hermes and walk the setup wizard">
+
+```bash
+curl -fsSL https://raw.githubusercontent.com/NousResearch/hermes-agent/main/scripts/install.sh | bash
+```
+
+The install script drops Hermes at `/usr/local/lib/hermes-agent/` and then launches an interactive four-question setup wizard. Answer:
+
+1. **How would you like to set up Hermes?** → **Quick setup**.
+
+![Hermes first-launch setup: Quick setup vs Full setup](/images/hermes-on-vps/hermes-on-vps-wizard-setup.png)
+
+2. **Select provider:** scroll to the bottom and choose **Leave unchanged**.
+
+![Hermes provider list with Leave unchanged selected at the bottom](/images/hermes-on-vps/hermes-on-vps-wizard-provider.png)
+
+3. **Select terminal backend:** **Keep current (local)**.
+
+![Hermes terminal backend list with Keep current local selected](/images/hermes-on-vps/hermes-on-vps-wizard-terminal.png)
+
+4. **Connect a messaging platform?** **Skip** (set up later via `hermes setup gateway`). You'll configure Telegram in a later section using the gateway wizard.
